The “Amphibian Modernist” Who Refused to Imitate
A giant of the Latin American avant-garde, Venezuelan artist Oswaldo Vigas helped define a modernism that resisted Eurocentric ideals.

GUANGZHOU, China — In a June 1985 article in the Venezuelan newspaper El Nacional , painter Oswaldo Vigas decried the exhibition Rauschenberg and the Third World , a traveling show organized by the Rauschenberg Overseas Culture Interchange (ROCI) program at Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Caracas. “Latin America, both in its literature and in its visual arts, has always been characterized by possessing its own languages, through which it expresses conceptions of the world and of humanity that have nothing to envy in those developed by those other societies,” the late Venezuelan artist wrote of Robert Rauschenberg’s paternalistic Cold War initiative. “If there is anything important I see in this exhibition … it is its value as an example of precisely what we Latin Americans neither should nor have any reason to imitate.”

A giant of the Latin American avant-garde who worked between his home country and Paris, Vigas, who died in 2014, helped define a modernism that resisted Eurocentric ideals. Instead, he favored experimentation that reflected Venezuela’s Indigenous past and a hopeful vision for the future. This struggle — and fusion — between aesthetics and culture is at the center of the Guangdong Museum of Art’s survey of the artist’s work, Reality Is What I Imagine .
Town Comes Together To Guide Child’s Medevac Plane After Runway Lights Broke
Town Comes Together To Guide Child’s Medevac Plane After Runway Lights Broke The remote village of Igiugig, Alaska, has given the world a masterclass in solidarity. Even more impressive…
Town Comes Together To Guide Child’s Medevac Plane After Runway Lights Broke
Photo: annavaczi/ Depositphotos (Not a picture from the actual event)

The remote village of Igiugig, Alaska, has given the world a masterclass in solidarity. Even more impressive, they did so despite only having a population of about 70 people. When a medical evacuation team couldn’t land at the local airport to help a child because the runway lights were broken, the city showed up, lining up their cars to guide the plane with their headlights.

It all started when Ida Nelson, head tribal clerk based in this small southwest Alaska village, heard a loud noise after 11:30 PM on August 28, 2020. “When they first flew over, I was like ‘oh my gosh,’ that sounds like a weird vehicle. I’ve never heard that truck before. And it wasn’t a truck, it was an airplane,” Nelson told KTOO . “Anytime there’s any type of planes flying after dark, you always assume it’s going to be something urgent and an emergency.”

And it was an emergency: a LifeMed Alaska crew was trying to land. When Nelson, who lives close to the airport, looked outside, she realized the runway lights weren't working. Worried, she got in her truck, where she met a local pilot who had also noticed the issue. While pilots can usually turn runway lights from their aircraft, that didn’t work this time. Nelson and the pilot also tried turning on the lights manually from the ground to no avail.

Concerned, Nelson offered to light up one end of the runway with her truck, but they still needed more help. And so, Nelson’s neighbor rallied the community, making 32 phone calls. Meanwhile, the pilot hopped into his own plane and contacted the LifeMed crew. “I was feeling nervous, anxious because this is late at night and this is someone’s child,” Nelson told CNN . “The only thing I could think of was how quickly I could get other people here to help because what if that was my baby’s plane?”

Within 20 minutes, 20 people had shown up in their vehicles, many in their pajamas, ready to follow the plane crew’s instructions. The townspeople staggered their cars and 4-wheelers along the runway so the pilot could see end to end. The people remained in place as the plane landed, boarded the patient, and departed safely for Anchorage, where the young patient made it to the hospital in stable condition.

While the LifeMed Alaska crew are no strangers to harsh Alaskan conditions, they were impressed by the community’s efforts to help one of their own. The team took one photo of the Igiugig runway lit up by its residents as they took off, and shared it on Instagram with the message, “It’s amazing what a community can accomplish with a little ingenuity and a lot of determination!”

These Tiny Fish Show That Evolution Can Happen Quicker Than We Thought

Evolution is typically thought of as a slow, gradual process, with species adapting over generations in response to environmental changes. But when environments change suddenly and dramatically, evolution can happen much faster than scientists once thought.

On March 27, 1964, a powerful earthquake struck southern Alaska , lifting parts of the coastline and creating new freshwater ponds from what had once been marine habitat. Several threespine stickleback fish became trapped in these ponds across at least three islands in Prince William Sound and the Gulf of Alaska, forcing them to quickly adapt to their new and very different environments. Isolated from other stickleback populations still in the ocean, the freshwater sticklebacks developed dramatically in less than 50 years.

Scientists from the University of Alaska Fairbanks, University of Alaska Anchorage, University of Oregon, and University of Illinois compared the newly adapted stickleback with older freshwater populations and found that, despite being less than 50 years old, they had evolved many of the same genetic and physical characteristics, including differences in their eyes, body shape, color, bone size, and body armor.

“We find that the freshwater populations, despite population genetic analyses clearly supporting their young age, have diverged phenotypically from oceanic ancestors to nearly the same extent as populations that were likely founded thousands of years ago,” reported the scientists in 2010. “Our results support the intriguing hypothesis that most stickleback evolution in fresh water occurs within the first few decades after invasion of a novel environment.”

This incredible discovery suggests that rapid evolution could be possible in other species, too. “This research perhaps opens a window on how climate change could affect all kinds of species,” said Susan L. Bassham, a Cresko lab senior research associate who co-authored the paper. “What we’ve shown here is that organisms—even vertebrates, with long generation times—can respond very fast to environmental change.”

Ferrari Is Dipping Its Toe Into Ocean Racing With Its New 100-Foot Flying ‘Hypersail’

Ferrari is synonymous with fast cars, but the company is expanding its fleet by dipping its toe into ocean racing. Hypersail is part of Ferrari ’s ambitious move into this form of professional competition, building on its automotive engineering expertise and the demands of high-performance team racing.

The Hypersail is a 100-foot flying ocean monohull, a sailing vessel with a single hull that’s the primary way it stays afloat. Moving a vessel this size above the water requires enormous lift, balance, and speed. Ferrari’s groundbreaking technology is designed to lift the giant vessel off the ocean surface. The team aims to break records and technological barriers. The project has generated 20 patents designed to solve problems involving energy generation, sail handling, aerodynamics, and controlling a 100-foot boat traveling above the water.

The secret behind Hypersail’s ability to rise above the waves lies in three underwater components: its foils, keel, and rudder. Together, these appendages generate lift, maintain balance, and respond to changing sea conditions. The foils act like underwater wings, producing the upward force needed to lift the hull out of the water and reduce drag. The keel incorporates an additional foil with a movable flap that helps manage flight and provides another point of support. Meanwhile, the rudder features a small movable wing that continuously adjusts the boat’s steering.

Hypersail’s flight control system draws on Ferrari’s automotive electronic systems and dynamic control expertise. It automatically analyzes environmental conditions like wind and waves, along with boat speed and heel angle or tilt, to keep the boat stable and balanced no matter the sea’s temperament. This also frees the crew to focus on reading the ocean, making strategic decisions, and finding ways to maximize performance.

Additionally, the racing yacht is designed for energy efficiency. It generates its own electricity using renewable energy sources, including solar panels and wind turbines, for greater self-sufficiency on long ocean voyages.

One of the project’s major long-term ambitions is to set offshore records, potentially including an attempt at the Jules Verne Trophy, the record for the fastest nonstop, unassisted circumnavigation of the globe. The first launch and sea trials are expected in 2027.

Unmaking the World With Jack Halberstam
The gender theorist’s latest book charts a constellation of artworks, critical theory, and science-fiction “unworlds,” particularly in the work of artist Gordon Matta-Clark and queer…

For decades, Jack Halberstam has been extolling the virtues of not doing what we’re supposed to — or not doing anything at all. In 2011’s The Queer Art of Failure , for instance, the pioneering gender and queer theorist posited failing as a form of creative resistance to capitalist concepts of success; in 2020’s Wild Things: The Disorder of Desire , he suggested “wildness” as a force of queer disruption to the status quo; and in 1998’s seminal Female Masculinity , he reimagined masculinity severed from maleness. His latest book, Anarchitecture After Everything: A Trans Manifesto (2026), treads further still into the terrain of queer opposition with a philosophy of unmaking and reorganizing the built environment, which he calls “unworlding,” in order to dismantle heteronormative social structures.

In contrast to “world-building,” which seeks to enact change within the parameters of these systems, Halberstam explains that “an unworld is not simply the opposite of the world we inhabit … An unworld must also unthink the logics of this world that make contemporary life under capitalism seem inevitable and right.”

The book’s thesis is summarized in its first sentence: “Anarchitecture, a set of art practices that emerged in the 1970s out of experiments with the sculpting of abandoned buildings, offers an expansive language for thinking about how bodies (and specifically trans bodies) emerge as a consequence of cutting, breaking, dismantling, and collapse.” Since space and bodies organize our daily lives and larger economic and sociopolitical sphere, “cutting” them isn’t just a symbolic act; as Halberstam writes, it’s about making “strategic cuts into the support system for our unfriendly climate and our racist world.”
Smithsonian American Art Museum Explores U.S. History Through 225 Photographs
Smithsonian American Art Museum Explores U.S. History Through 225 Photographs The Smithsonian American Art Museum brings together 225 photographs documenting the United States around its…
Smithsonian American Art Museum Explores U.S. History Through 225 Photographs
Robert K. Hower, July 4, 1976, Louisville, KY, 1976, gelatin silver print, Smithsonian American Art Museum, Transfer from the National Endowment for the Arts, 1983.63.789, ©1976, Robert K. Hower

The Smithsonian American Art Museum brings together 225 photographs documenting the United States around its 1976 Bicentennial in Much Here Is Beautiful: Photography Surveys of the U.S. Bicentennial . Featuring work by more than 70 photographers, the exhibition spans the country, from New York City to rural Appalachia. Together, these images capture communities during a period of social and economic change.

The photographs grew out of a federal initiative launched by the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) to mark the nation’s 200th anniversary. Inspired by the Farm Security Administration’s documentary photography during the Great Depression , the program funded 72 regional surveys of American life. The exhibition reunites selections from these projects for the first time, including works rediscovered through curatorial research.

Much Here Is Beautiful also traces the history of federal survey photography. It opens with 19th-century images by Carleton E. Watkins, Timothy O’Sullivan, and William H. Jackson, whose photographs introduced many Americans to the West’s landscapes. Works by Dorothea Lange and Walker Evans show how documentary photography later expanded to record everyday life.

The exhibition spans four regions, from Lee Friedlander’s photographs of industrial towns in the Northeast to Robert Townsend Jones Jr.’s previously unseen images of Beale Street in Memphis. In the Midwest, Joel Meyerowitz photographs St. Louis and its Gateway Arch, while John Margolies documents the roadside attractions that define the American landscape.

In the West, Mark Klett and JoAnn Verburg revisit historic landscapes through their Rephotographic Survey Project, placing contemporary images alongside 19th-century photographs. Reagan Louie’s photographs of San Francisco’s Chinatown offer a more personal perspective on the communities and histories that shape the country.

The exhibition takes its title from Robert Hayden’s 1978 poem “American Journal.” The phrase offers a fitting lens for photographs that look beyond familiar national symbols. Instead, they document the people, places, and everyday experiences that shape American life. Seen together, these images preserve a portrait of the country while inviting viewers to reconsider how its history has been recorded.
Much Here Is Beautiful: Photography Surveys of the U.S. Bicentennial will be on view at the Smithsonian American Art Museum in Washington, D.C., through April 18, 2027.

Here’s What a Perfect Game of Checkers Looks Like, According to Researchers

People have been playing versions of checkers for thousands of years, making it one of the oldest board games still played today . But despite its long history, researchers only recently figured out what happens when the game is played perfectly.

In 2007, a team led by University of Alberta computer scientist Jonathan Schaeffer announced that checkers had been weakly solved ; if both players make the best possible move every time, the game will always end in a draw.

Reaching that conclusion took nearly two decades. Beginning in 1989, Schaeffer and his team used computers to analyze the game, eventually building databases containing around 39 trillion endgame positions. That might sound excessive for a game played on an eight-by-eight board, but checkers is far more complicated than it looks. Researchers estimate around 500 billion possible positions. Rather than calculating every single one, the team worked from both ends. They solved huge numbers of possible endgames while their program searched forward from the standard starting position until the two sets of information connected.

At the center of the project was Chinook, a computer program originally created to compete against the world’s best checkers players. It eventually became strong enough to outperform human opponents, but Schaeffer and his team wanted to go one step further and prove what would happen if both sides played without making a single mistake.

That’s where the term “weakly solved” comes in. The researchers did not solve every possible checkers position. Instead, they proved the outcome from the normal starting position and showed that neither player can force a win when both play perfectly. Of course, that doesn’t mean every game of checkers will end in a draw. Human players make mistakes all the time, leaving plenty of opportunities for someone to triumph.
So while checkers may be mathematically solved, it isn’t exactly ruined. Unless both players can play perfectly, there’s still plenty of game left to play.

Feast On This Art World Roast
Hyperallergic skewers the art world and serves it up for your Thanksgiving feast. Also, artist Kohar Avakian eulogizes the ancestor whose legacy lives on.

This year, as the American holiday takes on new levels of monstrosity amid USA 250 propaganda, we’re marking it in the best way we know how: with a healthy serving of gratitude and satire. Let’s start with the second one — because what’s Thanksgiving without a pageant? Enjoy our full art-world roast, starring MoMA as the sad, white turkey meat and the Breuer Building as the dreaded turducken. Dig in!

Meanwhile, artist and scholar Kohar Avakian approaches the day by turning her attention toward a figure whose life was largely left out of the historical record: Cuff Annum. The enslaved Black man, who would serve in the Revolutionary War, became a common ancestor for a lineage of African-American and Native families in Massachusetts. Avakian, one of his descendants, lingers on the archive’s failure to capture his legacy and answers that gap with her own visual art.

And in the spirit of gratitude, we asked artists, art workers, and other community members we know to reflect on what they’re thankful for as 2026 draws to a close. Writer Christina Sharpe sums it up best: “All of the ways of being for each other when fascism wants to individuate, hierarchize, and isolate fill me with gratitude.” And we’re thankful for you, dear reader, wherever you are today.

Yes, it’s a day to be surrounded by those you love, even if some topics may be taboo at the dinner table. But what’s love without conflict? Hyperallergic is not one to appease those who deserve a light ribbing, particularly in an art world that prides itself on being so cutting-edge and consequential — for better or worse.

So, we’ve chosen to whet your appetites a little before your big meal by roasting our dear art community and reminding us all that laughter and humor are integral to how we digest the world and its many foibles and maddening realities.

The Budapest-based illustrator fills her colourful drawings with curious characters and unexpected details, encouraging us to slow down and find joy in the everyday.

Spend a few minutes in Réka Mátyás ’ portfolio, and you’ll meet two spotty dogs gazing at each other across a green meadow, a polka-dot cat posing beside an equally polka-dot tabi shoe, and a woman with ladybugs crawling through her golden hair. Polka-dot sisters, three cats stretched out across a chocolate-brown page, and a figure cradling a birthday cake with a single lit candle appear. It all feels soft, warm and slightly odd, splashed in a playful palette of bubblegum pinks, grassy greens and buttery yellows.

The Budapest-based illustrator and motion designer was born in Transylvania, Romania, and began her creative journey at university, where she studied Fine Arts and graduated with a BA in 2022. She experimented with all sorts of materials and mediums, though pencil sketches and realistic drawing were her real loves. By the end of her degree, she admits, she “felt quite lost”, with plenty of pressure to find her own style. So she took a year off and landed a role at a small creative studio as a motion designer, where she picked up the software, dabbled in graphic design, and started to see new possibilities. That led her to Budapest for a master’s in Graphic Design, which she completed in 2025. Today, she works full-time as a motion designer at Artbinary, “an amazing agency where I feel like part of the family”, while illustration fills her free time, along with the occasional graphic design project when something resonates.

For a long while, Réka felt she had to pick one path out of the three. “It stressed me out quite a bit,” she says. “But over time, I’ve learned to embrace all three, and I finally feel like I’ve found my place. I’ve also realised that switching between them keeps me creatively fresh. Each discipline gives me a different perspective and a little breathing room from the others, allowing me to return to my work with new ideas and push it in directions I might not have discovered otherwise. Now, rather than seeing these different paths as competing with each other, I see them as things that feed into and strengthen one another.”

With the world around her as her muse, Réka’s ideas usually come from everyday moments. “I’m interested in observing people, their lives and the little moments that might seem insignificant at first,” she says. Réka then jots these observations down or makes quick sketches in a notebook, where an idea might sit for months before it finds its way into an illustration. Nature, music, films and whatever book she’s reading chip in too, because “you just have to pay attention and stay curious”.

When the time comes to make something, Réka sits quietly for a few minutes and lets her mind wander, imagining a little scenario around the theme. Then comes lots of tiny, rough pencil or coloured-pen sketches. “They’re usually pretty ugly, and I almost always hate all of them at first!” she laughs, but this messy stage is where the final concept tends to appear, often somewhere completely different from where she started. Once something feels right, she plays with the composition, mood and colour, then moves to her iPad, which she says is usually the quickest part.

Among her favourites is an illustration for ZEITmagazine, commissioned by art director Viola Hasse, and her first editorial job. She had never drawn older people before, so she dived straight into sketching, starting with the couple at the centre – looking lovingly into each other’s eyes – and building a story around them with symbols and perspectives. Look closely, and you’ll spot a bird with a broken wing, which denotes the woman’s gradual loss of independence; pills; a pair of glasses; a water droplet and a character looking longingly in the distance. “I wanted the storytelling to feel subtle, rather than too literal, with little details that you could discover as you looked at the image,” she says. “I really enjoyed finding ways to translate the different layers of the story into small visual elements.”
Pattern Coffee is what happens when a Belfast branding studio becomes its own client
Fluent Format’s David Lewis on Pattern Coffee, the Belfast speciality coffee brand he’s built with Andile Cebekhulu as a side project, and what it taught them about clients. I’m a big fan…
Fluent Format’s David Lewis on Pattern Coffee, the Belfast speciality coffee brand he’s built with Andile Cebekhulu as a side project, and what it taught them about clients.

I’m a big fan of side projects. Creative Boom began as one, and look at it now. It seems I’m not alone. Every studio has one. The passionate thing on the side that gets talked about on a Friday afternoon, sketched out on paper, and then quietly forgotten about when Monday’s deadlines come in.

David Lewis and Andile Cebekhulu actually made theirs come true. David is the founder and creative director of Belfast brand and digital consultancy Fluent Format; Andile is its lead developer. By day, the pair build brands and digital experiences for other people. Alongside all that, they’ve been finding the time to build Pattern Coffee, a speciality coffee brand of their own.

Much like my platform, it began with no plan to be a business at all. The two friends spent nine months sourcing and trying coffees from around the world before deciding there was an opportunity. “We’re both dads with young families, busy jobs and a real love of coffee,” says David. “We joke that coffee is what keeps us going, but it’s also something we genuinely enjoy.”

What’s with the name, though? It came about during a phone call after work, when the pair got talking about how coffee had become part of their daily ritual – a moment to step away, reset and go again. Cue Pattern, along with a brand philosophy, ‘Your daily sweet spot’.
Graphic designers spend their working lives telling clients that brand matters. So can you imagine the pressure when it’s your own name on the packaging, and your own money behind it?

“We’ve always believed that a great brand can make a real difference to a business,” says David. “It’s not just about having a nice logo or packaging. It’s about creating something people recognise, connect with and want to be part of. Pattern gave us the chance to connect with and want to be part of. It gave us the chance to explore that from the very beginning, with complete creative freedom.”

I’m familiar with that freedom. It lets you go crazy without constraints. For David and Andile, it showed up most in the packaging. Because rather than go for the usual coffee tin, they developed a sleeve that follows the same silhouette of the bag, so the overall shape stays the same while each batch of coffee gets its own visual identity.
“We knew how the bag looked on a shop shelf was just as important as how it looked on someone’s kitchen counter,” explains David. “We wanted to create something people would enjoy having around.”
Wings, rugby and a snowball effect

Amazingly, there’s been no traditional marketing. Instead, Pattern has grown through small brand activations, like collaborations with running clubs and gyms, and even pop-ups at chicken wing shops – not, I admit, where I expected a speciality coffee brand to show up. But there you go.
The pair has also sponsored grassroots rugby, including women’s sports events, schools and universities, and supported Cancer Fund for Children on several occasions.

“We’ve found that the smallest things often have the biggest impact,” says David. “One collaboration leads to another, someone discovers the coffee and shares it with a friend, and before you know it, there’s a real snowball effect. It’s allowed us to build the brand and community we always wanted, without forcing it.”

But speciality coffee can feel intimidating when you think of all the tasting notes and brew ratios. Pattern is having none of that. “We love good coffee, but we don’t think you should have to know everything about it to enjoy it,” David continues. “We wanted Pattern to feel approachable, welcoming and something everyone could be part of.”

So what are the lessons from running a coffee brand on the side when you build brands for a living? Quite a lot. “It’s been a proper hustle getting it off the ground,” says David. “When you’re the one sourcing products, packing orders and investing your own money, you develop a completely different appreciation for the start-up founders you work with.”

Portsmouth’s August bank holiday festival had a bit of a problem. Too many people were buying a ticket for one act on one day, then disappearing. Wildish & Co.’s solution is an identity that puts the city first.

Who doesn’t love a good festival? I’ve been to my fair share over the last thirty years, and I can always tell you which bands were playing. The Prodigy in 1995 and Bowie in 2000, both at Glastonbury. Cypress Hill at V Festival in 2022 along with Asian Dub Foundation, I think it was. Björk at Bluedot a few years ago. Fun times.

If you’re running an event like this, you’ll know a lot hangs on your line-up. If it isn’t good enough, people simply won’t book. Victorious Festival knows this only too well. For more than a decade, the three-day event on Southsea seafront has drawn crowds from across the south of England, including Kings of Leon, Jamiroquai and Kasabian. But many of those only bought a ticket for a particular day, saw their fave act and went home. As such, each day felt like a different crowd, and that transience can be hard to build a community around.

Cue London agency Wildish & Co., which has given Victorious a new brand strategy, verbal identity and visual system that helps sell the festival as more than its line-up. Yeah, the headliners are still there - Black Eyed Peas, Pet Shop Boys and The Kooks are on the 2027 bill – but they’re no longer the sole attraction. Portsmouth is.

The idea is to sell the weekend , not just one day or act. Which is why the new positioning makes sense: ‘The People’s Classic’. It’s a line inspired by the ones who keep coming back, from families and festival veterans to traders, volunteers and first-timers. A second line, ‘Portsmouth Says Welcome’, ties the brand to the city that hosts it. Perfect.

It’s smart because you can’t own a line-up but you can own a seafront, a city, and something to look forward to every August. It’s something no rival festival can compete with. If you shift the story from who’s on stage to where you actually are and who you’re with, then a day ticket starts to look like you’re missing out.

The history behind the festival is also lovely. Victorious grew out of Portsmouth’s own music scene – its founders previously ran local venue Little Johnny Russell’s – and the new strategy includes a celebration of those humble roots.

Going back to the warm welcome, who’s it for? The identity launches alongside the 2027 line-up with large-scale posters at London Waterloo, Clapham Junction and Brighton, which shows you the target market.

Looking at the logo, it swaps the O in Victorious for a starburst borrowed from the sun on Portsmouth’s own coat of arms. Will you look at that – the city is quite literally in the middle of the name. The starburst also acts as an icon and is used across social, merchandise, wristbands and wayfinding.

There’s a custom headline typeface called Victorious Bold, which has tall, narrow capitals which stand out beautifully on everything from posters to stage screens. And the palette is taken right off the seafront – Navy, Sky, Sunset and Sunrise colours are complemented by secondary hues such as Sun Burn, Sea Spray and Sea Weed. A wave device runs through the lot, framing tickets, flags and signage. This was clearly a fun brief.

Then there are the illustrations, drawn in an engraving style and celebrating people enjoying themselves: a crab in headphones, for example, plus a sandcastle built from speakers and a seagull in a bucket hat. Remember those? Bucket hats were very handy when you needed to roll something out of the wind. Ahem.

A really nice touch is that every artist’s press photo gets a custom risograph-inspired treatment, so every act looks like part of the same thing. In other words, the headliners have been made to fit into Victorious’s world, when it has previously been the other way round.

Is the client happy? “Wildish & Co. got Victorious straight away,” says Leah Hennessy-Williams, head of PR and marketing at the festival. “They understood that what makes this festival special isn’t just who’s on stage, it’s the sea air, the city and the people who come back every single year. The Glasgow studio built the Edinburgh company’s brand from the ground up, from naming to rackets.

If you haven’t heard of padel yet, don’t worry: your life will be fine without it. At the same time, it’s nice to know that this trendy racket sport, which is kind of a cross between tennis and squash, is making a lot of people very happy right now; mainly in North America, but increasingly in the UK too.

Inevitably, there’s already a crowded market of kit brands all competing for padel fans’ attention. And the latest to catch our attention, at least, is CCO: an Edinburgh-based startup aiming to become a premium international padel brand.
This new brand has been crafted from the start by Glasgow studio Freytag Anderson, four-time winner of Scottish Design Agency of the Year.

Their work has included naming, positioning, visual identity, product architecture, racket design, and packaging, while for the website and e-commerce side, they teamed up with Form , a studio based in Aberdeen and Glasgow.

Readers of Creative Boom might read CCO as “Chief Creative Officer”, but that’s not what most padel players will think in practice. In any case, the name here is an acronym for “Control Creates Opportunity”. That will make perfect sense to fans of the game, where patience and placement tend to beat brute force.
The overall positioning of the brand, meanwhile, blends technical performance with a refined, lifestyle-led feel. This is captured simply but precisely in the tagline: “Performance. Synced.”

At the heart of the visual identity is a stepped typemark inspired by the movement of a padel ball. The two Cs and the O read almost like frames from a slow-motion replay, as if the ball is gradually coming into focus.

It’s a simple idea, but it’s been executed brilliantly, and is flexible enough to stretch across the brand’s three racket ranges, along with balls, apparel and accessories. The design particularly comes to life on the rackets themselves, where the mark is stacked, mirrored and multiplied to create bold, radiating patterns that echo the rhythm of the game.
A similar use of pattern repetition carries across to the campaign images, captured by photographer Beth Chalmers, in which players appear in staggered, multiple-exposure frames.

The colour palette – mostly blacks, whites and greys – evokes an understated, premium feel. This, along with the clean, sans-serif typography and restraint, helps the brand stand out in a sporting category not known for its subtlety.

“For the digital experience, we brought in Cameron Fraser and Kyle McKenzie at Form Digital ,” says Daniel Freytag, creative director at Freytag Anderson. “They’re exceptionally good at what they do, particularly when it comes to creating thoughtful, intuitive digital experiences that also work commercially. Together we translated the brand into a Shopify-powered e-commerce platform.”

Which museum is a white-meat turkey, which is a sad side salad, and who's riding the gravy train this holiday season?

Yes, it’s a day to be surrounded by those you love, even if some topics may be taboo at the dinner table. But what’s love without conflict? Hyperallergic is not one to appease those who deserve a light ribbing, particularly in an art world that prides itself on being so cutting-edge and consequential — for better or worse.

So, we’ve chosen to whet your appetites a little before your big meal by roasting our dear art community and reminding us all that laughter and humor are integral to how we digest the world and its many foibles and maddening realities.

The Museum of Modern Art’s refusal to let go of its billionaire trustee is the saddest, yet least surprising thing ever. A museum birthed and continually fed by the ultra-rich and their scions might be the poster child of neoliberal America, no matter how many women-focused, BIPOC, or queer programs they support in what essentially is a “let them eat cake” approach to equity. But cake is too sweet for this lot, even if its richness may be fitting, so we’ve decided to give them the plump spot of white turkey meat on today’s roast. Like the tryptophan-rich poultry, MoMA’s political hypocrisy makes us want to take a nap.

Nothing ruins Thanksgiving like a bland, butterless, suspiciously pale lump of mashed potatoes; perhaps the same is true of Alma Allen’s soulless sculptures at the just-closed Venice Biennale. The spineless presentation at the United States pavilion was the (tasteless) product of the State Department’s reported involvement in the art exhibition. All that’s left to say is: Pass the salt!

Though it's a beautiful deep berry color, there’s always too much cranberry sauce — and when it’s passed around the table, everyone politely says, "No, thank you." That’s why we deem Pace Gallery to be the cranberry sauce: There are too many locations, too many pretty colors, and no one wants any of it, especially the 50 staffers and 50 artists who were laid off and cut from the roster this June.

Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos
In 'The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse,' the British-Turkish photographer captures a portrait of the region's living heritage.

Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia , a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse , photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak , which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.
The book is available for purchase directly from Hemeria , and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram .

Andrew Hopgood is an Australian artist from Melbourne whose practice brings together illustration, oil painting and sculpture. Having started his artistic journey in illustration, he expanded into painting and sculpture around 2019, developing a visual language that combines realism with subtle surrealist elements. Much of his work centres on the natural world, particularly endangered species and the challenges wildlife faces as its environment continues to change. Through carefully constructed compositions, Andrew captures the beauty and presence of animals while drawing attention to their vulnerability and the importance of protecting the world they inhabit.

A defining feature of Andrew’s work is the way he blurs the boundaries between reality and fantasy. His compositions often place familiar elements of nature within imagined settings, creating scenes that feel at once recognizable and otherworldly.

These dreamlike environments allow him to explore the environmental pressures affecting wildlife while also considering the possibility of adaptation and survival. Rather than focusing solely on the loss and uncertainty surrounding endangered species, He introduces subtle moments of hope, imagining a natural world that continues to find ways forward. Through this balance of realism and imagination, he encourages viewers to look more closely at the relationship between humans and the environment, and to consider the role we play in shaping its future.

Joa Vilallonga’s paintings explore liminal states beyond linear time, opening visual fields where stillness becomes active. Working within contemporary figuration, she approaches portraiture as a psychological landscape. Her figures merge subtly with their surroundings, inhabiting states of silent depth. Rooted in a self-contained feminine presence, they neither seek approval nor resolution; vulnerability and strength coexist without performance.

Natural elements such as water, wind, gravity, and light function as compositional forces. Water plays a central role in her imagery, suggesting fluidity and receptivity. The human form appears permeable, shaped by transitions that soften boundaries and slow perception. Animals and small organic forms act as quiet counterparts, grounding what cannot be directly spoken.
Through restrained composition, muted palettes, and subtle luminosity, she builds contemplative images that invite sustained attention while leaving interpretation open.

In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. “We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by Olafur Eliasson , Marshmallow Laser Feast , and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their Instagram .

Helen Bur’s Monumental Bordeaux Mural Celebrates Motherhood and Female Solidarity, France
British street artist Helen Bur completes her largest mural to date in Bordeaux's Grand Parc neighbourhood, celebrating motherhood, female solidarity and community connection through EXIT's…

British street artist Helen Bur has completed her largest mural to date in Bordeaux, France, transforming the towering façade of the Nerval residential building in the Grand Parc neighbourhood into a monumental portrait of motherhood, female solidarity and human connection. Entitled Matrescense , the artwork depicts two local women in the final trimester of pregnancy, brought together through a project that celebrates the importance of companionship and mutual support within the community.
Helen Bur, WIP, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The title, Matrescence , refers to the profound transition into motherhood, a developmental process encompassing the physical, psychological, emotional and social changes experienced as a woman becomes a mother. Much like adolescence, it is a period of transformation in which identity, relationships and perceptions of self evolve.

Through her portrayal of two expectant mothers, Helen Bur gives this often overlooked experience a monumental public presence, recognising not only the vulnerability and anticipation of pregnancy but also the importance of connection, understanding and mutual support during one of life’s most significant transitions.
Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Created for KIFKIF, an ambitious urban art initiative led by Bordeaux-based association EXIT, the mural marks the beginning of a wider programme connecting internationally recognised artists with local residents through public art, creative workshops and community participation.

At the heart of Matrescense are two pregnant women arranged head-to-foot, their bodies forming an intimate, almost circular composition reminiscent of the yin-yang symbol. One reclines towards the ground while the other turns upwards, their opposing positions creating a sense of balance and interdependence. Although each woman occupies her own space within the painting, their gestures and proximity suggest an unspoken relationship built upon understanding, companionship and mutual care.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

Both women live in Bordeaux’s Grand Parc neighbourhood and were invited to become models for the artwork. Remarkably, they had not known one another before the project, making their connection something that developed through the creative process itself. What appears to be a longstanding bond between two women was, in fact, formed through the experience of participating in the mural.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The subject emerged from Helen Bur’s exploration of the neighbourhood’s social realities, particularly the experiences of women raising children without a partner. Rather than portraying motherhood through an idealised image of the family, she places two expectant mothers together, acknowledging the friendships, relationships and wider networks of support that can become essential throughout pregnancy and parenthood.
Matrescense: Intimacy on a Monumental Scale

Rising across the façade of the Nerval building, the 32-metre mural transforms an ordinary residential elevation into an expansive, deeply personal painting. Completed following more than two weeks on site, despite challenging weather conditions, the work represents a significant milestone in Bur’s artistic practice.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

The composition is particularly striking for the contrast between its monumental scale and the intimacy of its subject. The two women appear suspended within a richly layered interior of deep terracotta, warm ochre and patterned textiles, surrounded by abundant green foliage. The arrangement creates the impression of a private domestic space opened to the city, allowing an everyday moment of connection to occupy the architecture of an entire building.
In detail: Matrescense, Helen Bur, Bordeaux, France, 2026. Image copyright Association Exit

OUTSIDE IN: New Exhibition at GraffitiStreet Gallery, Chichester
What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? OUTSIDE IN brings internationally recognised street artists to GraffitiStreet Gallery, Chichester, exploring…

What happens when art made for walls, rooftops and railway lines comes indoors? This November 20th, GraffitiStreet Gallery presents OUTSIDE IN, a group exhibition bringing together internationally recognised artists whose practices are rooted in graffiti and street art. Exploring the journey from public space to the studio, the exhibition considers how an artist’s distinctive visual language moves between different settings, scales and materials, and how these transitions change the way we experience their work.

A graffiti tag, a mural spanning a building, a canvas contained within a frame and a sculpture within the gallery each create a different encounter with the viewer. Site can amplify or redirect meaning, scale can alter our response, and material can reveal another dimension of an artist’s practice. Yet across these shifts, the symbols, ideas and signature styles that define each artist remain unmistakable. How much of urban art is bound to its setting, and how much travels with the artist?
As the street enters the gallery, OUTSIDE IN invites visitors to discover what changes, what intensifies and what endures.

German artist Case Maclaim , a pioneer of photorealist graffiti, moves between monumental murals and intimate studio paintings, bringing the technical precision and extraordinary attention to detail that have defined his practice into a more concentrated setting.

Spanish duo PichiAvo unite classical sculpture and graffiti, bringing ancient mythology into dialogue with contemporary urban culture. Their distinctive compositions challenge the boundaries between artistic traditions, allowing the language of the street to coexist with the enduring influence of classical art.

South African artist Faith47 , internationally recognised for her poetic large-scale murals, extends her practice into sculpture, exploring how familiar themes and imagery acquire a different physical presence through material and form.

British artist My Dog Sighs transforms overlooked objects and unconventional surfaces into emotionally resonant artworks, while Sweet Toof brings the irreverence of his unmistakable teeth motif into paintings that connect graffiti, portraiture and art history.

Belgian artist Joachim Lambrechts balances spontaneous mark-making with carefully considered compositions, while South African artist Sonny Sundancer explores the expressive possibilities of abstraction beyond his large-scale street practice. Nean Kingdom , whose distinctive imagery has become an instantly recognisable part of his artistic identity, similarly demonstrates how a visual language developed through street art can retain its character in the studio.

Although their approaches differ considerably, each artist offers a perspective on the relationship between artistic identity and environment. Moving between the street and the studio becomes more than a change of location; it creates opportunities to experiment with materials, reconsider scale and develop ideas beyond the conditions in which their practices first emerged.
An Exhibition Across Materials and Disciplines

Alongside the featured artists, OUTSIDE [IN] includes selected artworks and collectables by Banksy, STIK and TOX, bringing further dimensions to the exhibition’s exploration of graffiti and street art.

From the repetition of a graffiti tag to the intimacy of a painting, the exhibition reveals how urban art continues to evolve across disciplines while retaining its connection to the visual culture of the street.

Together, these diverse practices create an opportunity to experience familiar artistic languages in an entirely different context, encouraging visitors to look beyond the surface and consider the ideas, techniques and identities that give each artist’s work its distinctive character.

JM Brea Paints the Moment Before the Crucifixion in Montehermoso
JM Brea has painted La Crucifixión del Cristo de los Remedios outside the chapel of the Santísimo Cristo de los Remedios in Montehermoso, Spain. Made for the town council, the mural stops…

JM Brea has painted La Crucifixión del Cristo de los Remedios outside the chapel of the Santísimo Cristo de los Remedios in Montehermoso, Spain. Made for the town council, the mural stops just before the first nail is driven through Christ’s hand. Brea places the moment of impending violence beside a chapel whose altar holds an image of the crucified Christ.

In Brea’s account of the composition, Christ’s hand rests against the wood of the cross while a nail is held over its palm. The action has not yet happened: the pointed nail and the waiting hand carry the tension. Brea describes the treatment as Baroque in character, a choice tied to the chapel rather than simply to the biblical subject.

The painting also draws on details at the site. Three nails represented at the top of the main altarpiece find an echo in the mural’s single poised nail and the shadow of three fingers across the painted wood, according to Brea. Outside, three granite crosses stand near the chapel. These connections give the work a particular setting: its scene begins on the exterior wall, while the crucifixion appears in the sculpture inside.

Montehermoso’s town council dates the chapel to the 16th century and describes it as regional Baroque in style. The image of the Cristo de los Remedios inside is from the 18th century. The chapel remains associated with the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and devotions to Christ of the Remedies, making Brea’s subject closely bound to the building’s use as well as its decoration.

The mural is part of Vientos del Pueblo, a literary and cultural route developed with Montehermoso’s schools and local partners. The project links artistic work in the town to education and local heritage. Brea’s contribution is grounded in one place: the chapel, its crosses and the image encountered within.

The work extends across multiple sides of the downtown Elm Street parking garage, where Beyond Walls curated a public-art project for the city. Across town, Mr. June painted the High Street garage. Together, the commissions form Nashua in Motion, a project developed by Beyond Walls with the city and architecture firm Payette.

Work on the garages began on September 14 and concluded on October 2, 2026. Beyond Walls led the painting phase after preparations for the two structures, with the artists working on active downtown facilities rather than isolated mural walls. At Elm Street, the building’s corners and successive elevations make the painting something visitors encounter in stages as they move around the garage.

That relationship between a work and its surroundings has long been part of Eltono’s practice. In an artist statement published by Beyond Walls, he describes public space as a place of unpredictable conditions that affect what an artist makes. His Nashua painting puts that practice on a conspicuous piece of city infrastructure, though the statement does not prescribe a reading of this particular composition.

At a walkthrough marking the end of the painting period, Eltono told Nashua Ink Link, “What we did is pretty incredible in such a short time.” He also described hearing encouragement from people passing the site as the work took shape. Oli-B Paints With His Left Hand for the Fêtes de la Saint-Martin in Beauvechain

Oli-B has painted an abstract mural in Beauvechain, Belgium, for the 2026 Fêtes de la Saint-Martin. He calls the experiment The Left Hand Project: he made the wall painting entirely with his left hand, setting aside the precision and control that usually guide his work.

The change was physical before it was visual. Oli-B says he worked with larger masses, textures and movements, allowing his gestures and the paint to lead. He describes the exercise as a way to embrace unpredictability, while still paying attention to how colours meet, shapes balance and the composition holds together.

That balance is central to the Brussels artist’s wider practice. His paintings and murals bring fluid forms and emphatic colour into carefully constructed arrangements. For this wall, changing hands did not mean abandoning those concerns. As Oli-B puts it, the experiment is “a shift in approach, rather than a departure from my visual language.”

The mural was made for the 60th Fêtes de la Saint-Martin, whose street-art programme is curated by Jaune and Marcela. Oli-B credits Jaune with inviting him. The organisers have placed murals on exterior walls across villages in the Beauvechain area, bringing an art form often associated with city streets into a rural setting. They say painting began in late October, ahead of the festivities running from November 8 to 29, 2026.

Oli-B’s mural is at 11 Rue de Louvain in Beauvechain. It is one stop on the outdoor route, but its working rule makes it a distinct test within his practice: how much can the movement of a hand change when the artist keeps his attention on the same questions of colour and form?

French street artist Seth Globepainter creates six murals across the Faroe Islands for We Need Art 2026, exploring childhood, migration, wildlife and the traditions that connect generations.

French street artist Seth Globepainter has created six murals across the Faroe Islands for We Need Art 2026 , drawing upon the archipelago’s maritime heritage, wildlife and cultural traditions to explore childhood, migration and belonging. Set against dramatic coastal landscapes, working harbours and familiar village architecture, the paintings bring Seth’s distinctive visual language into dialogue with the lives of the people who inhabit these North Atlantic islands.

Through images of children, seabirds and symbolic encounters, the series considers what it means to leave home, to imagine a world beyond it and to preserve the traditions that connect one generation to another.
Seth Globepainter’s Puffin mural in the Faroe Islands, depicting a boy wearing a puffin mask offering a sand eel to a bird with a human mask. Image copyright Julien Malland.
Puffin: A Meeting Between Two Worlds

In Puffin , painted in Kollafjørður, a young boy wearing traditional Faroese clothing and a puffin mask offers a small sand eel to a puffin wearing a human mask. The figures face one another in an unusual exchange of identities, their shared gesture suggesting an attempt to understand the world from another’s perspective.

The painting takes inspiration from the relationship between humans and nature in the Faroe Islands, where fishing, seabirds and the surrounding waters have long shaped everyday life. Seth approaches that relationship through a reversal of familiar roles, allowing the child to assume the appearance of a bird while the puffin takes on human characteristics.

For the artist, the encounter is concerned with harmony, adaptation and empathy. Rather than portraying people and wildlife as separate inhabitants of the landscape, the exchanged masks suggest the possibility of recognising something of ourselves in another living being.

The mural’s setting reinforces that connection. Painted on a harbour building, with the waters of the fjord and surrounding mountains visible alongside it, the work occupies the environment from which its imagery is drawn. In one photograph, a young child wearing traditional Faroese dress sits beneath the painted figures, creating an unexpected relationship between the artwork and the living culture it represents.
Seth Globepainter’s Puffin mural in the Faroe Islands, depicting a boy wearing a puffin mask offering a sand eel to a bird with a human mask. Image copyright Julien Malland.
Taking Flight: The Distance Between Childhood and Home

The emotional complexity of leaving home emerges in Taking Flight , where a seated boy watches a young girl rise into the air. Painted on opposing sections of weathered concrete, the two figures are physically separated by a gap in the structure, transforming the existing architecture into an essential part of their story.

Seth connects the painting to the migration of Faroese people who leave the islands in search of employment and opportunities elsewhere. The departing girl becomes a figure of possibility and separation, while the boy who remains watches a departure he cannot prevent.

The artist also draws upon the relationship between Peter Pan and Wendy in J. M. Barrie’s novel, introducing another interpretation concerned with the loss of innocence and the passage from childhood into adulthood. The girl’s flight carries both the excitement of discovering another world and the sadness of leaving something familiar behind.

Positioned among rocky ground, vegetation and residential buildings, the figures appear almost absorbed into their surroundings. The distance between them, emphasised by the physical break in the concrete, gives the painting a quiet emotional force that might have been lost on an uninterrupted wall.

Masters of disguise: the insane tactics the Stasi used to monitor their targets

One came dressed as an athlete. One as a ballerina. Another as a footballer. Another as a judge. All looking like they are having the most awkward time one could possibly have. You’d think that was just the feeling of trying to have a good time in East Berlin before the Cold War ended, but this was something different. These were all members of the Stasi.

For those lucky enough not to have encountered this delightful slice of bleak Cold War paranoia, the Stasi were the East German Secret Police. They were tasked with keeping a strict eye on anyone even suspected of having sympathies with the capitalist pig-dogs of the West, lest they make a break for the other side of the wall or, worse, start smuggling intelligence out of East Germany altogether. They were also a workforce, though. And workforces need to have their spirits up, so that photo I was describing above came from a costume party where each attendee came dressed as one of their targets.

Honestly, as terrifying as it sounds, I can kind of see it. How else would you get a group of people to ignore the horror of infringing on the dignity of strangers and their basic right to privacy other than by making a joke about it? Maybe with some pithy quips about how everyone at the party is monitored every hour of the day, so you’re not doing anything to them that you’re not going through as well. Har-har, everyone makes a show of laughing before going back to their drinks. They are being watched after all.

They’re being watched as much, if not more, than any of their quarry, and considering some of the utterly insane tactics used to keep track of Stasi targets, that’s saying a lot. This was an organisation that used to break into a target’s living space when they weren’t home, steal their dirty underwear and swab the seats of their couch in order to build up a scent profile of them that they’d store in a “smell jar”. This way, if they ever needed to urgently catch them, they could just open the jar in front of one of their attack dogs, and then the chase began. I’m not making any of this up.

This would be alongside the more traditional stuff like storing hidden cameras and microphones in their apartments, taking on disguises to follow them in public and recording every phone conversation they ever had. Here’s the thing, though, the vast majority of the time, these Stasi would just be monitoring people living normal lives. Those suspicions were often specious at best, drawn from extreme paranoia and a desperate need for control.

However, sometimes those people being tailed were just too suspicious to stay free. It didn’t matter that they showed no signs of defecting to the West or even that they particularly wanted to; they just had a sibling who lived in Paris , or they’d started seeing someone who used to live in West Berlin. That was enough to start the process of Zersetzung, quite literally “decomposition”. This would essentially be weaponised gaslighting, where the goal was to send a target insane.

This would be done by spreading rumours about them among their friends and family, sending numerous goods to their home that they never ordered, and sending anonymous letters that stated just how much whoever was watching knew about them. That was step one. After they were softened up, the real games began. They would break into their home while they slept and make subtle adjustments. Like changing their brand of tea, switching their furniture around and removing pictures from the walls.
They’d also make sure to remove those previous letters, just to make them sound even more crazy to everyone in their life.

This wasn’t just cruelty for the sake of cruelty (at least in their eyes, it totally was in practice). Because being arrested for no reason would make someone a martyr. If they seemed to go completely insane and just had to be taken in by the state, well then that’s just a sad state of affairs, nothing to be suspicious about. Perhaps after all that, it wasn’t actually that difficult to make the Stasi themselves OK with doing this to their countrymen.
After all, if there was the slightest sign they weren’t, it would start happening to them.

How alcohol, gambling and prostitutes turned a beloved doctor into “the shame of Minneapolis” in 1901

Just because someone has done good things in their time doesn’t mean they’ll be good in politics . We’re known this long before the days of Albert Ames and his time as mayor of Minneapolis in the early 20th century, yet the reasons he sums up that argument so perfectly are still distressingly relevant today.

Ames was known to most in his native Minneapolis as ‘Doc’, and this wasn’t just a nickname. He became a respected man about town first as a veteran of the Civil War and then as a doctor and surgeon. Not only was he skilled, but his reputation was also for being a kind and understanding soul. He would treat poor patients without charge, answer calls at any time of day or night and was one of the first responders on the scene in 1886 when a deadly tornado ripped through St. Cloud and Sauk Rapids.

Now, it’s worth mentioning that these could be additions to his reputation put in by Ames and his administration after he came to power later in life. However, people did believe in him enough to support his political aspirations fairly soon after the Civil War came to an end. The only issue was that Ames did so as a Democrat at a time when Republicans controlled Minnesota. While he was an exciting, well-liked candidate who people had earmarked for power, his early political career was pockmarked by failed grabs for higher power.

Even when he did win a few terms as mayor of Minneapolis in the late 1870s and 1880s, he was nothing special and soon eclipsed by other candidates. This was devastating for Ames, who had a desperate, all-encompassing need to be liked. That, and a drinking problem that was getting worse by the year, drew him closer to the city’s criminal underworld. By the end of the century, Ames was a liability who’d been left behind by the state’s Democratic Party, so he did what any washed-up has-been would do who had one last shot at making something of himself.
He switched to the Republican Party and ran a campaign supported by his criminal buddies.

Ames squeaked out a victory and, in 1901, began a term in office where he essentially ran the city the way a crime boss would. He replaced nearly every member of Minneapolis’ nascent police force with thugs from the criminal underworld on his payroll, setting up his drinking buddies in prominent positions of influence around the city and hiring his brother Fred, possibly even more of a failure than he was, as his right-hand man.

Ames was done trying to work for the city, so he made Minneapolis work for him. He bussed in card sharks and con artists from out of state and allowed them to work in the city so long as a cut of their earnings went to him. The same went for the City’s brothels, speakeasies and gambling dens; they could all operate with police protection for a fee and Ames, fittingly enough, made out like an absolute bandit.

At the time, Ames’ predilections were an open secret around town; he was just too valuable to his cronies for anyone to get anything to stick. At least until 1902, when a grand jury from out of state sent a team of private detectives into the city. With national authorities breathing down his neck, there was no way to pay off the people who got their hands on hard evidence showing that Ames had taken bribes from every crook in the city. Especially after that grand jury indicted a number of Ames’ cronies, including his brother.

At first, the coward tried to run, but was caught and convicted of bribery in 1903. Ames had too many friends in high places for the conviction to stick, and it was overturned on a technicality the same year. However, the damage had been done. Everyone finally knew that Albert Ames was a crook, and his actions led to several dramatic overhauls of Minneapolis politics, increasing the scrutiny on his successors to make sure that nothing so nakedly criminal would ever happen again.
Once upon a time, Albert Ames might have been a good man. His legacy, though, would be as “the shame of Minneapolis.”

The horror movie so extreme its director was arrested for murder in 1980
Much was made of The Blair Witch Project’s epoch-defining marketing campaign, which people said was the first of its kind attempted in movie history.

Put simply, the movie was promoted like it was found footage taken by three students who disappeared on a hike in the woods of Burkittsville, Maryland. The first promotional material for the film was a website about the “missing” students that addressed them by the actors’ real names. This was followed by other websites about the legend of the Blair Witch and the countless other people who’d gone missing looking for her. It was hailed as a masterpiece of marketing that no one had ever tried before… which wasn’t strictly true.

In fact, 20 years earlier, a film had tried to present itself in a similar fashion, as actual found footage of something horrifying that had somehow secured a mainstream release. Not only did it work, it worked so effectively that the exact opposite thing happened to it. The movie was so convincing as an actual document of real violence that it kneecapped the movie and nearly got its directors thrown in jail. One can only imagine what it must have been like to watch an early screening of Cannibal Holocaust and start thinking, ‘Wait, is this actually real?!’

Even without the idea that what you’re watching is real, the Ruggero Deodato-directed and Gianfranco Clerici-written grindhouse classic is a brutally tough watch. One that the producers of the film really leaned into, going so far as to get the actors to sign a contract after the film was released, preventing them from working again for a full year to maintain the illusion that everything on screen had actually happened.

Thus, when the film premiered in Milan in February 1980, a local magistrate got hold of it and immediately ordered the arrest of Deodato. However, this wasn’t just because of the supposed treatment of the actors in the film.

Now, here is the actually complicated part of Cannibal Holocaust’s history, which is that the film really did kill six animals on screen in scenes of unsimulated slaughter. It wasn’t simply that the actor’s death scenes looked uncannily realistic for the time; it was the fact that no one had seen them since work on the film had finished and that the director did have scenes of actual animal death in the film.

This caused Deodato, along with several of the film’s producers, to be arrested on obscenity charges and suspected murder. They had to bring the cast to court to prove they were alive, and even then, there was one shot that the authorities were suspicious of. The iconic shot of a character impaled lengthways on a wooden pole, the top end poking out of her mouth. The authorities quite simply didn’t know how that could be achieved without actually doing the act itself, and Deodato had to explain the shot in detail in court.

All they’d done was sit the actress on a bicycle seat attached to an iron pole, positioned the camera so the seat was hidden, then placed a piece of balsa wood in her mouth and told her to tilt her head up. Needless to say, the production team of the movie was cleared of all murder suspicions, though they still had to go on a high-profile Italian TV show with the cast to prove to the country they weren’t dead. However, the obscenity charges stood, and the creative team were handed suspended prison sentences, large fines, and the movie was banned all over Europe.
The price of being ahead of your time, I guess.

The truth behind Mary Shelley losing her virginity on her mother’s grave in 1814
It’s a pretty spectacular twist of history that Mary Shelley ended up being more famous and renowned than her husband.

Percy Bysshe Shelley was one of the truly notorious figures of his day, probably second only to Lord Byron himself in the mad, bad and dangerous-to-know stakes. Considering that The Right Honourable One was the man for whom that term was coined to describe, that’s saying something.

However, Shelley was a notorious figure in his own right, mainly due to his passionate atheism back when it was actually a controversial point of view that could get you ostracised from society. Y’know, around 150 years before Ricky Gervais was even born.

In fact, it was that atheism that indirectly caused him to meet the woman he would later marry and get completely eclipsed by in terms of cultural influence. Writing a pamphlet on the subject while at Oxford caused Ol’ Perce to get expelled , so Shelley went on a writing spree, contacting everyone he’d ever considered an influence to see if they could mentor him further. One of the people who got back in touch was Mary’s father, William Godwin.

Over the next few years, Percy and William became confidantes. They were so close that when Shelley was set to inherit a colossal personal fortune, he took notice of Godwin’s mounting debts and offered to pay them all back interest-free. This turned Shelley from a friend of his to something of a son to him, and the young aristocrat became a fixture of their table, where he became friendly with Mary.

Despite Mary coming from one of the most alternative families in the country, her parents being notorious radical thinkers, William wasn’t comfortable with his 21-year-old financial lifeline hanging out with his 16-year-old daughter. Nevertheless, Mary and Percy were captivated by each other and found numerous reasons for the two of them to go on long walks around London, where Mary showed him her favourite reading spot. St Pancras Old Church, right next to her mother’s grave.
Yeah, she would later go on to invent horror fiction; why do you ask?

This was a scandalous bond at the time. While the age gap is disconcerting today, it wasn’t at the time. It wasn’t even simply the fact that Shelley was courting the daughter of someone financially beholden. It was the fact that Shelley was already married. Yet that was a relationship that had long since fallen apart, and the feelings Shelley and Mary had for each other were very mutual. So much so that on one of their trips to Mary’s mother’s grave on June 26th, 1814, Mary confessed her love for Percy.

Which is where you might think that the part of this story you’ve definitely heard about happens. That Shelley took Mary’s virginity on top of or against her mother’s grave. It’s scandalous. It’s vile. It’s probably romantic to a very specific type of person who’s spent way too much time watching Tim Burton movies. It’s also almost certainly bollocks. Not just because neither of the two parties involved wrote about it in their diaries or letters, either.

The clue people took to was a casual, flippant mention of Percy’s, where he said that he felt like he had a “new birthday” when Mary confessed her love to him. So-called historians then had boatloads of fun speculating on some disgusting gossip about two of the more famously salacious people of the time. The theory falls apart even further when you consider that not even the gossips or commenters of the time said anything about it.

Not because they were too prim or unimaginative to imagine it either. After all, barely a month later, Shelley and Mary eloped with Mary’s stepsister Claire Clairmont. Within two years, those same gossip commenters were going wild with reports that the three were a throuple they proudly referred to as the “League of Incest”. Our minds aren’t any dirtier than they were in the 1800s, yet there wasn’t a single mention of a graveyard tryst . Just a man ecstatic that someone that he loved, loved him in return.
Who was five years younger than him and 16 years old, mind. Best not lose sight of that.

‘London After Midnight’: How the first fan film in 1927 preserved movie history
Never be afraid to make things.
These days, movie making is so accessible that actual directors are making entire films out of the kind of technology freely available to all.

You don’t need to be a movie studies scholar to know that this is a far, far cry from how the industry was even three decades ago. In fact, this was one of the key ways that the industry was gatekept from others. It quite simply wasn’t something one could just do with a few bob in their pocket and a can-do attitude; you really needed the approval of people who worked in the industry just to do something that looked anything like a real motion picture.

However, that wasn’t to say that the occasional unauthorised movie didn’t slip through the cracks. The majority of those didn’t emerge until the 1950s and 1960s, when actual home recording equipment began hitting store shelves.

Before then, you had to have serious money in order to make anything work without the say-so of the film industry, which must have been the case in 1927, when a horror-loving couple saw the Lon Chaney-starring horror classic London After Midnight .

This was long before any kind of home media, but that wasn’t enough for this couple, who were so taken with the picture that they decided to recreate a scene of it themselves. This being a couple based in The Hamptons, they clearly had the money to not only rent out a full-on movie camera just for their lark, but also to take the time and effort to give the typically incredible Lon Chaney make-up work down enough to serviceably recreate it on their own terms.

Thus, they got started recreating their favourite scene in the picture on 16mm film with a friend of theirs standing in for Chaney’s character. It’s a charming lark the way that vast majority of fan films are, but little did the creators of this film know that a few decades after they finished work on their charming lark, it would actually become a vital piece of cinema history. In 1965, an MGM vault containing the last known print of the film burnt down.

This made the fan film the best resource people had to work out how the movie looked on screen and in motion . The only remaining parts of the movie are its posters, some promotional stills and a remake of it with sound from 1935 called Mark of the Vampire . However, what we can learn from this fan film goes much deeper than mere technical aspects. We also learnt how popular the film was at the time. Because it’s actually kind of difficult to tell what films from the 1920s were really beloved or not.

We didn’t even have the box office receipts because film releases didn’t really work the same way back then compared with today. All we know officially is how many cinemas rented reels for the film from MGM, which isn’t quite the same as gauging its effect on the public.

This fan film, probably made at a shocking cost for the time, shows us that not only were these films popular, but they were truly beloved. They made people go out of their way to recreate them at a time when a lot of very powerful people were working very hard to make sure that people literally couldn’t do that.

A sign, if one was needed, to embrace the things you love and create things inspired by it. You never know how important a cultural document of something may be until it’s too late, and then, you too could be a very literal part of cinematic history.
