Gloria Steinem was booked up. There had been luncheons and interviews scheduled for the fall; a high-profile conversation with Katie Couric at 92NY and a prominent place in The New Yorker Festival’s lineup. She left appearances unfulfilled, interviews unaired, an essay unpublished and a forthcoming book. In short: Gloria Steinem was, at 92, far from done.

That energy is palpable in that very book, her memoir An Unexpected Life , published on September 22, in which she states that she planned to live to at least 100. Although she was “older than [she] ever imagined,” mortality didn’t really cross her mind much. Any why would it, when she was also “happier than [she] ever imagined” and her calendar was bursting at the seams? Part memoir, part manifesto, part consciousness raising group, An Unexpected Life is a collection of essays in which Steinem reflects on her life, lays out her worldview and looks towards the future. And just as she was in life, on the page she radiates a matter-of-fact conviction and an unflinching clarity—the result of more than sixty years spent organizing a movement.

Her story begins long before she would become the most prominent face of second-wave feminism (although Steinem would reject this label), with a bruised childhood in Toledo, Ohio. She spent stretches of her young life on the road, until her father left when she was ten years old, leaving her in a rat-infested home caring for her increasingly mentally ill mother. With a childhood spent longing for warm kitchens and cookie cutter family units, it is striking that Steinem would grow up to spend so much of her adult life traveling around the country, more often than not living out of a suitcase. But even more formative than her earliest years, perhaps, was the time spent in India in her early 20s, an experience that would become the very foundation of her feminism.

Although mortality was far from Steinem’s mind, it is apparent in these pages that she was hyperaware of her legacy. “At my age, in this still hierarchical time, people often ask me if I’m ‘passing the torch,’” she wrote in her 1983 book Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellion s . “I explain that I’m keeping my torch, thank you very much—and I’m using it to light the torches of others.”

She is doing just that in An Unexpected Life , a text bursting with a kind of hopeful exhilaration about what could be. “Nothing is more exciting than making the invisible visible. It’s like finding the end in a ball of yarn,” she wrote. “Pull on it, and gradually the whole of patriarchy unravels.” At times, she gets as literal as bullet-point lists on how to best organize a feminist movement. There are glimmers of the—often cited—shortcomings of the women’s movement that she was at the helm of herself. “Insist on multiracial women who represent the movement,” is one such takeaway of Steinem’s. “Otherwise, people will have a distorted view.” There is an added poignancy to the essays upon her passing; a book that is as much about her life as it is a handbook for movement building. “Whatever my story might be to other people,” Steinem wrote, “I hope something has ripple effects that I myself may never see.”

One such ripple effect concerns her beloved home, an apartment in a brownstone building on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. “If time and ingenuity allow,” Steinem wrote in the book’s prologue, “I hope to acquire the other floors in this house and leave this whole building as a refuge for diverse women who need a place to stay or just to meet.”

Steinem first moved into her apartment in 1968, together with a roommate. Throughout the years, the apartment grew not only in square footage but in function. The single unit became an entire floor, which became three floors. Her living room had been a meeting place for over fifty years, where she hosted gatherings and talking circles up until this very year. She held meeting on topics ranging from women’s health to misinformation in the media—a meeting in that very living room had led to the founding of Ms. Magazine in 1971. The Radicalization of Eugene V. Debs and the Country He Radicalized in Return
On a foggy September morning in 1877, Eugene Victor Debs adjusted his suit collar and set out for the Indiana State House.

On a foggy September morning in 1877, Eugene Victor Debs adjusted his suit collar and set out for the Indiana State House. Just shy of twenty-two years old, he’d been a member of his labor union, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, for barely two and a half years. But today he would deliver the opening address to its national convention.

Horse-drawn wagons and carriages rolled through the downtown streets of Indianapolis, clacking on the cobblestones and kicking up gravel as paved stretches came to an end. Lavishly ornamented cast-iron buildings mingled with simple brick structures; steam whistles sounded from the railroad tracks bound for the teeming Union Depot, the first in the country to bring all train traffic to a central hub. City leaders were thinking longterm here. Meatpacking was the city’s other big industry, Kingan and Company’s mammoth plant one of the largest in the world, its state-of-the-art chilling system allowing year-round production in these days before refrigeration.

Indianapolis wasn’t Chicago or St. Louis, Midwestern metropolises with populations in the hundreds of thousands, but its 75,000 inhabitants painted a smaller-scale picture of a rapidly industrializing America. With all the corresponding possibilities and cruelties. The boom-and-bust of capitalism had gone bust four years before in the so-called Panic of 1873, an economic disaster nearly as severe as the Great Depression of the 1930s—and joblessness persisted in Indianapolis, as elsewhere. Workers terrified of being laid off grudgingly accepted wage cuts. Politicians responded to calls for a public jobs program with creative new punishments instead: fines for begging, a proposed workhouse “where all persons incapable of paying fines” would be forced to smash stones to pave more city streets.

Soon, Gene Debs would have seen the Indiana State House come into view. A white wooden fence edged the tree-lined lawn—the trunks like matchsticks, branches draped with green leaves holding on despite the imminent change in seasons. The dome of the state capitol rose above, a grand if crumbling structure of blue limestone and gray stuccoed columns patterned on the Greek Parthenon. Debs—amiable and outgoing, a bit over six feet tall, with a slim but solid build—entered the capitol and mounted the stairs to the House of Representatives’ chamber on the upper floor, which the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen was borrowing for the convention. He greeted his fellow delegates, who had exchanged their soot-stained work clothes for suits and ties.

Theirs was grimy, dangerous work. Firemen shoveled the coal that powered steam engines into the locomotive’s firebox, which was prone to explosion. Every month the firemen’s magazine carried grim news of widowed wives, orphaned children, maimed railroaders. Train derailments and collisions were ubiquitous. Railroad workers made up the bulk of workplace injuries in Gilded Age America: by one count 56 percent of the broken ribs, 50 percent of broken arms, 41 percent of broken legs, 71 percent of severed arms, and all of the amputated legs.

Nearly one in four trainmen could expect to die on the job if he worked for thirty years; only coal mining was as lethal. The work was well paid by the standards of the day, with veteran engineers often able to own their own home, but shifts were long and irregular, running anywhere from twelve to twenty-four hours, or longer. “It is no uncommon thing,” one railroader said, “for an engineer to go for nearly a week without sleep except in snatches on the road or waiting on a branch or engine house.” Workers lived close to the railyards, knowing that at a moment’s notice they could be gone for days or weeks. The imperatives of their employers, rather than their own individual wants or collective needs, governed workers’ lives.

Not that Debs begrudged the railroad companies. If the work was too dangerous or too demanding, the hours too long or the bosses too harsh, it was up to railroad workers to prove themselves worthy of more respect. The Map of Ancient Philosophy: Animation Shows How Socrates, Aristotle, Confucius, the Buddha & Other Great…
Here on Open Culture, we’ve often featured the charming and informative posters of Domain of Science. Each one maps out a different field of knowledge: there’s biology, physics, chemistry…

Here on Open Culture, we’ve often featured the charming and informative posters of Domain of Science . Each one maps out a different field of knowledge: there’s biology , physics , chemistry , quantum physics , quantum computing , fungi , and many others besides. But with his latest map, Domain of Science creator Dominic Walliman has turned away from the scientific realm — or rather, he’s ventured into the larger intellectual territory out of which it emerged. His new Map of Philosophy , which he explains in the video above , includes schools of thought going all the way back to 600 BC, and thinkers from antiquity like Thales, Laozi, Confucius, and the Buddha, who lived and died before science as we know it.

That hardly means that they’ve become irrelevant today. There still exist societies described as Confucian or Buddhist, of course, but in the Western world, we’re more likely to refer back to — and, in many cases, have read a bit of — the work of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. “They basically laid the intellectual foundation of Western philosophy, science, and political thought,” says Walliman. (He also reminds us that it was Socrates who said that the unexamined life is not worth living, which “hits pretty hard in the age of the distraction economy.”)

Though often mentioned together, these three ancient Greeks occupy slightly different positions on the philosophical map, with Socrates closer to the land of ethics, Plato to metaphysics, and Aristotle to epistemology.

As Walliman explains, “epistemology studies knowledge: what it is, where it comes from, and also how it differs from faith or opinions,” while also seeking out its limits. Aristotle’s rigor in testing and organizing knowledge makes him, in a sense, one of the earliest scientists. Though his body of theory may no longer be our best means of understanding how the world works, his systematic pursuit of such an understanding set him apart from much of the ancient intellectual world. The islands off the coast of the map’s mainland represent subfields still actively explored today, like the philosophies of mind, language, politics, religion, and science — which, for all its prestige, remains as subject to philosophical inquiry as any other area of human endeavor. The map of philosophy shows us not a rarefied, mostly abandoned territory, but the place where we all live our lives, examined or otherwise.

Fingers, frozen to the bone in the damp cold, barely obey.

A trembling hand fumbles in the scratchy wool of an overcoat pocket for another five-round clip. That damned bolt again. The last round stuck fast. One strike. Another—with a numb palm. New clip…stiff bolt handle forward and down…chamber a new round and close the breech.
So cold. Eyes ache from peering into the fogged dark. The head throbs from gunfire crackling since morning.
A minor railway stop, Kruty, lost in bleak fields, near a nameless hamlet beyond Nizhyn.

“They’re coming, still coming, stay alert!” officers shout hoarsely from the snow-covered embankment, voices strained. Through icy fog and under the dim light of a veiled moon, shadows advance across the wide field, cut through by endless rails.
The Reds send another wave into the attack.
A flash splits the darkness on the far horizon. Then a boom, and an explosion close by. The blasts throb like a pulse in the temples.
Teeth clench. The head pulls inward, wishing never to hear and see, shrapnel whistles overhead. This time for sure.
A hoarse shout—the machine guns burst to life, tearing the darkness with short volleys, chewing through belts of cartridges.
Around, thin lines of defense stretch across the silvery ribbon of rails: a motley battalion of whoever God sent, in whatever they had, with God knows-what instead of proper weapons.

Students from Kyiv. Young cadets in old overcoats, in felt boots, with grimy yellow-blue armbands on their sleeves. Gymnasium students, mere schoolboys who had hardly ever fired a shot before, in ordinary clothes, standing off to the left to keep away from harm. Fiery, dreamy lads who did not run, too ashamed to turn their backs.
So this was the revolution, marching from Petrograd, for the people’s happiness, of course. Cutting down the “old world” in its path, reeking of strong liquor.

One student—his face still untouched by a razor—keeps nervously adjusting his round spectacles again and again, brushing frost-dust with trembling fingers. They had all volunteered. Shivering in the cold, breathing heavily. Clumsily digging shallow trenches. They weren’t meant to be here. Schoolboys, maybe good enough to haul ammo, nothing more. So they were sent to a “relatively quiet sector” of the front, but ended up encountering the main enemy forces.

A handful of junior officers, none over thirty, stand beside them in Russian army uniforms, their epaulets torn off, imperial cockades missing. This was the young army of the Ukrainian People’s Republic—its most devoted part.
“Matviy, keep an eye on the youngsters here!” A gloved hand claps his shoulder, and the officer ducks low, moving on to steady the thin line.

Another deep, dull thud, one that rings sharp in the skull, not just the ears. The soft stubble of a cheek touches the frozen wooden stock again. Lungs pull in frost. Another shot into the darkness merges into the deafening cannonade. And another. And again.

They keep coming with bayonets fixed, advancing toward the machine guns across the field to the station. Navy peacoats, quilted jackets, caps, red armbands. They’ve been coming since morning. Sailors of the Baltic Fleet. Red Guards from Petrograd and Moscow…no strangers to this kind of work.
There they lie, bastards. Dozens of black mounds, sprawled in the dark after a day of relentless charges—frozen mid-agony, a bullet still in the gut.
The Reds are advancing on Kyiv.
So this was the revolution, marching from Petrograd, for the people’s happiness, of course. Cutting down the “old world” in its path, reeking of strong liquor.
Kharkiv is lost, Poltava is lost, Chernihiv is lost. Through forests and steppe, along rails from Russia, the armored trains grind toward the Ukrainian capital.
Another heavy blow from the Bolshevik battery—and now they’re pulling him away: sotnyk Omelchenko, the student company leader, his head torn open by shrapnel, blood gushing from beneath his cap.
You won’t make it to Kyiv, friend. Remember us up there.
We can’t hold this alone. Not for long.

Finding My Way in the Wilderness with Brush and Pen
In 1994, as a refugee from New York City advertising (an accidental career resulting from a failed attempt to convert my biology degree into artistic fame in the big city), I returned to my…

In 1994, as a refugee from New York City advertising (an accidental career resulting from a failed attempt to convert my biology degree into artistic fame in the big city), I returned to my home state of Vermont and dove headlong into wildlife art, crisscrossing the U.S. for six years on the national art show circuit. I didn’t write anything but birthday cards to my daughters.

Right in the middle of a show out west in the winter of 2000/2001, it hit me: I’d become as much a teamster as an artist, and I felt cut off from what inspired me to paint. I ditched my late summer schedule and planned an August/September, 330-mile “source-to-salt” canoe trip on the Missinaibi River, which flows north to James Bay (I bought my first canoe with my paper route money when I was 11). The trip wasn’t to be an escapist adventure, but work: a painting trip and a chance to reconnect with my Muse, as a classicist would say.

It also introduced writing into my creative repertoire. Realizing that hardly anyone would notice if I disappeared into the wilderness for a month, I contacted an art magazine that liked the artist-on-a-canoe-trip angle, and a canoeing magazine that liked the canoeist-on-an-art-trip angle. I wasn’t sure what I would write, but I figured something would come to mind on the river.

I’d assumed I’d have to go alone with an artist’s itinerary, but at an art show opening in June, John Pitcher, a pre-eminent U.S. wildlife artist, asked to join me. On the river, John and I became fast friends and discussed future trips, but in Mattice, Ontario, after 130 miles, he had to return, and I continued solo.

As soon as Mattice disappeared behind a bend, the enormity of what I was doing settled in. I was alone, facing 200 miles of wild river through roadless wilderness. On the one hand, I was keenly aware that without anyone to help, even a minor mishap could cascade into tragedy. On the other, the river held my undivided attention.
The wild expanses I have experienced aren’t alien places, but reminders that the wild is where we all come from.

That first night alone, I camped at the Kettle Falls portage, and in a substantial blow to my self-image as an adventurer, I was hit with an acute attack of loneliness. I focused on setting camp and starting dinner, but I couldn’t shake the intense melancholy. Then the westering sun lit the river’s east bank with an evening glow. Hoping for another distraction, I set to painting while my dinner boiled. I had to work fast to catch the light, but before long (and to my pleasant surprise), the painting started to come alive. A surge of euphoria welled up out of nowhere and washed the loneliness away in a tidal wave so intense that, for a few moments, I wondered if I was OK. The weirdest part was a heartwarming sense of connection, not just to my surroundings, but to people—not anyone in particular, but everyone. I was never lonely on the river again.

That evening, as I dutifully recorded the day’s events in the journal the magazines had asked me to keep, I discovered that my new assignment was more than just a travelogue. The small painting that had precipitated one of the most intense emotional reactions of my life could, ironically, do nothing to describe or explain the internal transformation I’d undergone. But writing could.
The Way North – Kettle Falls, Missinaibi River . Acrylic field painting, September 4, 2001.

Over the next week, I made friends with Canada Jays and sandpipers, talked to rocks and various pieces of my gear, all of whom were generally supportive. On the other hand, an oblivious bull moose nearly killed me by accident, and a large bear looked like he was contemplating doing it on purpose.

But the river and forest offered only indifference. There was sound: birds, wind, the current along my hull or surging through rapids, but no noise and nothing I did seemed to matter. The ageless enormity of the planet pressed in, a wild Earth utterly unconcerned with humans, and as I thought back on the dizzying diversity of life that “Mother Earth” has birthed, provided for, and let pass away through the eons, I realized she is an impassive parent. But writing is hard to dramatize, and for the bespectacled dweeb in the small room who spends his days backspacing and muttering and making trips to the fridge just to stare into its faint light without seeing anything in particular, the tendency is to transpose professional anxiety to flashier arenas.

“If the point of End Zone is that sports are an imperfect and inevitable metaphor for war, the point of Amazons is, as DeLillo reminds us several times, that ‘athletes have bodies.’ Cleo’s body is spectacular, with what one lover calls ‘big-league boobs’; her face is just O.K. Sportswriters exert themselves in describing Cleo . . . The book consists mostly of discrete episodes of fantastically crisp DeLillian conversation before Cleo takes a new man to bed—in one case, literally dragging his unconscious body on a rug. ‘This is the second straight chapter that ends with sex and intimate lighting,’ Cleo remarks, at the end of the second chapter. ‘There is a huge tradition behind this, but I’m not sure I want to be part of it. There are other ways to end chapters and I’m determined to find some of them before too long.’ She doesn’t, really.

“If sports novels are usually about greatness, erotica is usually about power. In Amazons , this calculation is simple: Cleo has it all. There is none of the usual give-and-take, no real battle of the sexes on the ice or in bed. That she can skate with the boys is never in question, and not a source of particular stress. Cleo is very good at what she does, and yet she thinks about her job the way a store manager facing down Black Friday thinks about his: very little, when not on the clock, except occasionally to contemplate the coming violence.

“We may have queer culture to thank for the very fact that we’re reading Amazons in the first place. The Times report ed that DeLillo decided to reissue the book amid the buzz around Heated Rivalry and the clamor for hockey erotica. I would prefer not to believe this, because the rather lofty DeLillo of my imagination would never change his mind about a disowned book for such crassly commercial reasons. A major subplot of Amazons involves Cleo refusing to do an ad for a snack food because she prefers a different brand in real life. We are supposed to find this silly but righteous. Still, whatever made DeLillo reissue the book, I’m glad he did. Amazons is so bouncy, so immediately and frankly pleasurable to read, that it could be studied as an example of a book with no payoff which nevertheless leaves the reader satisfied. Amazons won’t teach you anything about womanhood or greatness or hockey, and will teach you only very little about various forms of male longing, an already overexplored subject. But perhaps that’s enough. As this accomplished sports novelist famously put it, ‘Longing on a large scale is what makes history.’”
–S. C. Cornell on Don DeLillo’s Amazons ( The New Yorker )

The Natural History of the Sea-Serpent

A lively review by Dr. Octavia Arbogad of The Natural History of the Sea Serpent, To which is added, a Sketch of a Serpent-Hunting Voyage , by Achabbu Zarxas, translated by Kailung Smirtha. Published in Koot-Hoomi’s Quarterly, New Lovegain, 1341.

The patron who does us the honor to take up this article, as a gentle preparative for an after-dinner nap, may, perhaps, pardon us for reminding them that the soft turquoise light of their sitting-room lamp is borrowed from the largest and most ferocious of known creatures; that the oil which turns night into day, and invests its power upon the steam-engines of our manufactories and rail-roads, once formed part of a vast and fearsome being whose heart sent out twenty or thirty gallons of blood at every stroke, through an aorta measuring more than two feet in diameter; and that the creature whose gigantic frame was nourished by this flood of life gamboled on the broad back of the World-Ocean, rejoicing in its strength, till the minuscule, mortal human, whose engines had grown hungry for the wyrms’ treacly ichor, made war upon the beast in its own realm, and left the enormous mass inanimate. Nor is every one acquainted with the dangers and privations borne by those who seek the terrible monster in its remote watery demesne. A serpent-hunting voyage often exceeds three years, and hardly ever occupies less than two. From the port of New Lovegain alone an average of seventy sail of fine ships, of a burthen ranging from three to four hundred tons, are annually on the look-out for the fattest of sea-serpents. The crews of these ships, which are fully provisioned for three years, and sail from New Lovegain at all times of the year, consist of from twenty-eight to thirty-three sailors and officers—including at least one sorcerer, typically a tempestarius also serving as navigational astrologer, which, after all, seems to us to be a very commendable species of mixed practice. As, for obvious reasons, there are in such expeditions “no more cats than can catch mice,” the mariner who has been afloat in one of these ships is pretty sure to turn out a crack specimen of their genus—a smart character, case-hardened to any climate, expert in all their professional duties—endued with imperturbable nerves and quick decision, eagle-eyed, and tyger-hearted.

All the sailors are, in point of fact, co-adventurers with the owner; for they go “on the lay”—that is, they have a certain share of the produce, instead of the ordinary money-payment. This arrangement, which sailors find eminently favorable to employment in the smoky labyrinths of New Lovegain’s rail-fed manufactories, can be ascribed to the influence of the Mazuraa cultus, particularly those clades which favor the worship of the Deep Goddess in Her incarnation as Gykylyk, Mother of Storms. Such teachings have long argued that the great serpents, being ex nihilo and tempore ruinae the creation of their favored goddess, therefore exist as the common property of humankind, who have worked for over a millennium to appease the deities’ displeasure. The rewards of the serpents’ oil, the sea-laborers have proclaimed, should then at least be shared equitably amongst the crew who procured the stuff.

The zeal with which this dangerous sea-hunt is pursued seems to take the strongest possession of the sailors’ minds; and one of their most usual modes of making a heavy hour light is sketching their favorite ship, serpents in various attitudes, and the hair-breadth escapes of their companions and themselves, upon the tooth or bone of one of the monsters whom they have seen die. One of the grandest examples of such craft I have seen was upon a ship that patrolled the waters between the southern New Lands and San Borondon, executed upon a yard-long tooth. Its panoramic image was of the fearsome creature from which it was plucked, pictured “in a flurry” and pursued by a spate of skiffs from a finely-detailed schooner, but pierced with almost as many darts as the fabled Archemedon Wyrm slain by the sea-monks of San Borondon in Ontic antiquity. Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted. What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate…
Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted.
What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound.

As in music, so in life: “Listen to the silence inside the illusion of the world,” Jack Kerouac wrote to his first wife turned lifelong friend in reckoning with the meaning of life , “and you will remember the lesson you forgot.”

Silence is the listening presence through which you hear the music of your own life, presence purified to become peace — a peace greater than joy and unburdened by understanding, a peace the other word for which may be love.

There is no piece of music that has scored more of my waking days and my writing hours than “Spiegel im Spiegel” by the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, whose virtuosity with sound springs from his relationship to silence — something he articulates with poetic concision in a series of reflections recently shared by his son:
Silence is always more perfect than music. You must simply learn to hear it. Silence is utterly full.
When we speak of silence, we must keep in mind that it has two wings: Silence can be both outside of us and within us.
The silence of our soul, over which even external noise has no power, is actually more crucial. But is also much more difficult to achieve.

A generation before him, Kahlil Gibran had captured this difficulty with piercing pointedness. “You talk when you cease to be at peace with your thoughts,” he charged in his timeless meditation on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself . Pärt puts it more gently:
One does not have to compose, one does not have to write a book.
If you do not speak, thinking, and even prayer, is clearer, and there is more space left over for love.
I have always felt that the quality of silence two people can share is one of the great measures of love — something the young poet Babette Deutsch captured beautifully a century ago:
Silence with you is like the faint delicious
Smile of a child asleep, in dreams unguessed:
Only the hinted wonder of its dreaming,
The soft, slow-breathing miracle of rest.
Silence with you is like a kind departure
From iron clangor and the engulfing crowd
Into a wide and greenly barren meadow,
Under the bloom of some blue-bosomed cloud;
Or like one held upon the sands at evening,
When the drawn tide rolls out, and the mixed light
Of sea and sky enshrouds the far, wind-bellowed
Sails that move darkly on the edge of night.

How to Touch the Nothingness Behind Everything: Kahlil Gibran on the Seven Selves

A self is a forest . A self is a ship . A self is an illusion , and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is a sum of selves , contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

Kahlil Gibran (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life , takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic The Madman ( public library | free ebook ).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated the Japanese concept of ma .)
In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven
selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:
First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years,
with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow
by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.
Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is
given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter
and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance
his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary
Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand
of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self
who would rebel against this madman.
Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught
was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is
I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell,
who would protest against serving this madman.
Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self,
the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without
rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is
Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who,
with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images
and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the
solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.
Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this
man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to
fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined
lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits
in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating
life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?

Union Veterans and the Bitter Aftermath of the Civil War
As the nation embraced reconciliation, former Union soldiers questioned whether their sacrifices had been in vain.

In the decade following the Civil War, many white northerners wanted nothing more than to put the carnage behind them and reunify the country. But, historian Brian Matthew Jordan writes, one group that generally wasn’t ready to forgive and forget was Union veterans.

Jordan writes that the returning soldiers found a society that was happy to hail them as heroes but often offered them little material support. Many employers refused to hire men who they believed were too mentally or physically wounded to function.

And veterans’ efforts to ask for more were frequently dismissed. In the summer of 1865, just months after the war’s end, The New York Times complained that returning military men “prefer to live by begging.”

But Jordan argues that the veterans’ anger was not just about their own needs. Many felt that efforts to move past the conflict insulted their sacrifices. Those who returned with disabilities, painful wounds, and post-traumatic stress were reminded constantly of the war, and some worked to remind their neighbors, staging mock battles on town greens to show the “stay at homes” what the fighting had looked like. One wrote that “the momentous events of less than ten years ago are too fresh in memory to be forgotten at the command of any party that may be benefitted by ignoring them.”
The images, diaries, and ephemera in Grand Valley State University’s Civil War and Slavery Collection reveal the cold realities of Abraham Lincoln’s world.

A prime symbol of this neglect for many was the Confederacy’s president, Jefferson Davis . Soon after the war’s end, one veteran wrote to President Andrew Johnson, saying that he believed he had been “spared to witness the close of this wicked and unjust rebellion” and would be honored to help build a scaffold for Davis’s execution. Instead, despite being accused of treason, Davis was released two years after the war’s end and became a symbol of the Lost Cause . One Union veteran from Massachusetts complained that he had lost an arm “in vain” since “Jefferson Davis is today a hero, and more care is taken of him than the soldiers who fought to preserve the Union.”

Jordan writes that the Grand Army of the Republic (GAR), which was founded in 1866 and quickly became a national organization with 2,000 posts, focused primarily on supporting veterans, widows, and orphans, including by lobbying for benefits. But it also protested the appointment of “rebels and traitors” to government offices that could have gone to former Union soldiers.
GAR soon became a controversial group, with some northern civilians arguing that its demands and remembrances kept too much bitterness alive and made it difficult for the country to move forward.

In some cases, military service had also introduced northern soldiers to ideas about racial justice that their neighbors back home didn’t embrace . While not every white veteran became a supporter of Black Americans’ rights, Jordan suggests that it wasn’t uncommon. As the planter class attempted to reinstate a system of virtual slavery with the Black Codes and vigilante violence, some wondered if they would end up having to fight the war all over again.

Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” will almost certainly come near the top. At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast marble expanse, interrupted here and there by an item of furniture that seems dwarfed by the surrounding emptiness. An odd staircase rises from one distant corner. It is not impossible that this vision, in one of the best-known French surrealist films, inspired the designers of the great hall of Xanadu in Citizen Kane .”

The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for their own short adaptation of Poe’s story , which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films , you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer and B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman . Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton celebrated in animation at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe , a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on the playlist in various forms: an early D. W. Griffith feature , the directorial debut of Jules Dassin , an animated short narrated by James Mason , a British psychological thriller , and a transposition into modern-day New Orleans . And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watching through all 25 of these films, consider watching the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Usher miniseries on Netflix — an entertainment platform that satisfies much the same appetites Poe’s stories have been feeding for nearly two centuries.

Marie Curie Became the First Woman to Win a Nobel Prize, the First Person to Win Twice, and the Only Person…
For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and…

For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Matilda Effect” to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film Hidden Figures have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, in footnotes .

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “ Floating University ” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

Curie and her husband Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Antoine Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity, in 1903. The second prize, in Chemistry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different sciences.

These are but a handful of achievements in a string of firsts for Curie: denied positions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, awarded the degree in 1903 by the Sorbonne , the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her examiners,” notes the site Famous Scientists , “were of the view that she had made the greatest contribution to science ever found in a Ph.D. thesis.” Three years later, after Pierre was killed in an accident, Marie was offered his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.

Curie succeeded not in the absence of, but in spite of the sexist obstacles placed in her path at nearly every stage in her career. After she received her doctorate, the Curies were invited to the Royal Institution in London. Only Pierre was permitted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Committee decided to honor only her husband and Becquerel. The Academy relented when Pierre protested. Curie fell victim to a wave of xenophobia and anti-Semitism (though she was not Jewish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famously in the so-called “Dreyfus Affair.”

In 1911, the year of her second Nobel, Curie was passed over for membership in the French Academy of Sciences . It would take another 51 years before the first woman, Marguerite Perey, a former doctoral student of Curie, would be elected to that body. That same year, Curie was persecuted relentlessly by the French press, the public, and her scientific rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physicist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s former students.

But no matter how many men in positions of power wanted to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more influential scientists and politicians who recognized the supreme value of her work and the need to help her continue it. After her second Nobel Prize, her native country finally recognized her with the offer to direct her own laboratory in Warsaw. Curie turned it down to focus on directing the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute of the University of Paris, which she founded in 1914, a major achievement and, again, only a small part of her legacy.

Curie is known, of course, foremost for her exceptional scientific work, but also for opening doors for women in science all over the world, though much of that door-opening may only have happened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t happened at all yet. "If we are to be true and worthy heretics, we need not only new heads, but new hearts, and, most of all, that new emotional imagination... begotten of enlarged sympathies and a more…

“If we are to be true and worthy heretics, we need not only new heads, but new hearts, and, most of all, that new emotional imagination… begotten of enlarged sympathies and a more sensitive habit of feeling.”
UPDATE 2025: This book is now back in print as the third title in Marginalian Editions .

When the Inquisition persecuted Galileo for advancing the rude truth that Earth is not the center of the universe, the charge against him was heresy — the same charge on which Joan of Arc was burned at the stake for her crusade for political reform. We have had many words for heretics over the epochs — rebels, radicals, freethinkers — but they have always been the ones to dislodge humanity from the stagnation of the status quo, to illuminate our blind spots, dismantle our unexamined biases, and jolt us out of our herd mentality. Without those devoted to seeing reality more clearly and possibility more wildly, we would still live in a world haunted by superstition and governed by dogma.

The power and dignity of this most courageous human mindset is what the pioneering classicist Jane Ellen Harrison (September 9, 1850–April 15, 1928), who brought the culture of Ancient Greece to the modern world, explores in her magnificent essay “Heresy and Humanity,” found in Alpha and Omega ( public library ) — the out-of-print essay collection that gave us Harrison on the art of growing older , published just as humanity was being dehumanized by its first World War.
The word “heretic” has still about it an emotional thrill — a glow reflected, it may be, from the fires at Smithfield, the ardours of those who were burnt at the stake for the love of an idea.

Heresy, the Greek hairesis , was from the outset an eager, living word. The taking of a city, its expugnatio , is a hairesis ; the choosing of a lot in life or an opinion, its electio , is a hairesis ; always in the word hairesis there is this reaching out to grasp, this studious, zealous pursuit — always something personal, even passionate… To be a heretic today is almost a human obligation.
In a sentiment Bertrand Russell would echo in timeless manifesto for freedom of thought , Harrison adds:
The gist of heresy is free personal choice in act, and specifically in thought — the rejection of traditional faiths and customs.

A century and a half after Emerson inveighed that “masses are rude, lame, unmade, pernicious in their demands and influence,” she considers what makes heresy so difficult yet so necessary to the health of society:

All traditional views are held with such tenacity, such almost ferocity, because they belong to the class of views induced, not by individual experience, still less by reason, but by collective, or, as it is sometimes called “herd,” suggestion. This used to be called “faith.” The belief so held may or may not be true; collective suggestion is not in the least necessarily collective hallucination. Mere collective suggestions — that is the interesting point — have the quality of obviousness; they do not issue from the individual, but seem imposed from outside, and ineluctable; they have all the inevitableness of instinctive opinion… Hence they are held with an intensity of emotion far beyond any reasoned conviction. To doubt them is felt to be at once idiocy and irreverence. Inquiry into their rational bases is naturally, and in a sense rightly, resented, because they are not rationally based, though they may be rationally supported. It is by convictions such as this that a society of the homogenous kind — a society based on and held together by uniformity — lives and thrives. To attack them is to cripple and endanger its inmost life.
Observing that the development of science is what pivoted heresy from damnable to desirable in society, Harrison contrasts sensemaking by empiricism with sensemaking by authority:

Science classifies, draws ever clearer distinctions; herd-suggestion is always in a haze. Herd-suggestion is all for tradition, authority; science has for its very essence the exercise of free thought. When Colorado Closed Its Border to New Mexico
An anti-immigrant stunt in 1936 helped propel a governor to the US Senate, despite its limited practical impact.

By the 1930s, the federal government was in charge of immigration, having centralized and formalized the ad hoc immigration regimes cities and states had developed during the nineteenth century. So it was news in April 1936, when Colorado Governor Edwin C. “Big Ed” Johnson declared martial law along the border with… the neighboring state of New Mexico. Johnson publicized his action as a blockade to stop a supposed “invasion” of “alien and indigent persons.”

When his earlier proposal to set up concentration camps for Mexican immigrant workers, who were pressing for higher wages in the sugar beet industry, came to naught, he hit upon the border blockade gambit. Political scientist Monica W. Varsanyi writes of Johnson’s “ classic example of political entrepreneurship ”:

Although his plans had little actual impact on Colorado’s agricultural labor market or welfare relief load, they resulted in an outpouring of public support, which he exploited in his successful run for the US Senate later in 1936.”

Beyond yet another precedent for the political benefits of racism and nativism, Johnson’s actions present a case study of racialization, the political and ideological process of race-making and the creation of color lines. The militarized race border between two US states, continues Varsanyi:

created circumstances in which the social boundary between who belonged and who fell outside of citizenship and belonging was both heightened and vigorously contested in this uniquely multi-ethnic region populated by Anglos, native-born Hispanics, Mexican immigrants, and Native Americans.

American citizenship had originally been granted to “free white” persons in the Naturalization Act of 1790. The territory conquered in the Mexican – American War added at least 80,000 people to the rolls of American citizenship in 1848 . These Mexican Americans and their descendants therefore were considered white in federal law. But this was a precarious whiteness. In the Southwest, Mexican Americans were second-class citizens. Regardless of de jure law, Anglos did not see them as white and treated them accordingly . “Juan Crow” segregation covered housing, education, and employment.

Varsanyi quotes Colorado resident and US citizen Filigonio Arellano, “During wartime and when they need my vote, white people call me an American. If I need a loan, I am Spanish. And if I’m applying for a job they call me Mexican.”

Nonetheless, Johnson’s blockade received a good bit of support from native-born Hispanics. These US citizens tried to distinguish themselves as “Spanish Americans” or “Hispanos” in opposition to Mexicans. “Spanish-speaking New Mexicans, elite and impoverished alike, rebuffed claims of mestizo , ‘impure,’ or ‘mixed’ blood by tracing their lineage back to Europe and Spain, not Mexico.”
Birth of A National Immigration Policy
Until the Civil War, regulating immigration to the US was left to individual states. That changed with Emancipation and the legal end of slavery.

There was some “solidarity between Hispanic and Mexican workers, mainly within the labor movement and religious communities,” but otherwise little sense of a “pan ethnic/pan-Hispanic solidarity or ‘Mexicanness.’”

Of course, to a racist, birthplace or citizenship hardly mattered. New Mexico residents who were US citizens who tried going north for work in Colorado’s sugar beet, railroad, mining, and sheep-herding industries, as they had for decades, found that they were classified as “aliens” and “Mexicans” and turned back.

The blockade only lasted eleven days. Pressure from the powerful sugar beet interests—who could not get white Coloradans to work under the industry’s brutal conditions—and rising tensions with New Mexico likely led Johnson to call it off. A marked increase in racism persisted long after, however.

Johnson himself would go on to serve three terms in the US Senate before becoming Colorado governor again in 1955. Behold the Most Detailed Painting in History: The Ghent Altarpiece
These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can…

These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a level of detail is unavailable in a museum, of course, but also difficult to access even if you owned the physical artwork in question. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured such luxuriantly digitized paintings as The Night Watch , Girl with a Pearl Earring , and The Garden of Earthly Delights . But there’s at least one celebrated work of Dutch masters whose viewing experience can never truly be replicated on the internet: the Ghent Altarpiece , also called the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb , by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.

After watching the video from The Gaze above, you’ll surely want to take as close as possible a look at the online Ghent Altarpiece , seeking out such highlighted details as the individual hairs on Adam’s beard, the realistically awkward expressions on the faces of the angel chorus, and the identifiable crucifixion scene pinned to a pilgrim’s hat.

But that may only stoke your desire to make a pilgrimage of your own, to Belgium, where you can see the real thing carefully placed in St. Bavo’s Cathedral. In the early fifteenth century, when that institution was called St. John the Baptist’s Church, its warden was the wealthy merchant Jodocus Vijd. Having endowed a new chapel, Vijd also commissioned the van Eyck brothers to create an altarpiece spectacular enough to secure him a spot in the afterlife. The result was one of the earliest masterpieces of oil painting.

Even apart from that designation (to say nothing of its being the most stolen work of art in history ), it has enjoyed an impressive afterlife of its own. Of the many who have traveled to behold it in situ at St. Bavo’s, some have no doubt sought the ecstasy of faith that can only be felt in a true holy place. But others have been thrilled, whether they were aware of it beforehand, by all the attention the artists put into integrating the work with its surroundings. The light within its images, for example, is painted in such a way as to match the light streaming into the cathedral itself. Those who look closely at the gem worn by the foremost singing angel will see a reflection of the very room meant for the altar. By the time their eyes meet the knowing gaze of the sacrificial lamb, they’re all but guaranteed to have a religious experience — though whether its nature is Christian, artistic, or otherwise will depend, as it does with all enduring art, on the individual viewer.

How Isaac Newton Lost $3 Million Dollars in the “South Sea Bubble” of 1720: Even Geniuses Can’t Prevail…

The Aristotelian notion of “man” as a “rational animal” has seen its share of detractors, from the Cynics to Bertrand Russell to nearly the whole of Poststructuralist thought. Leave it up to Oscar Wilde to compress the debate between intellect and passion into a pithy aphorism: “Man is a rational animal who always loses his temper when he is called upon to act in accordance with the dictates of reason.”

We no longer need clever verbal barbs to refute too-optimistic assessments of human behavior. Economics is catching up: we have the language of neuroscience and psychology, which consistently tells us that humans decidedly do not behave rationally very often, but are driven by bias and biology in inexplicable ways . And for over a hundred years now, we’ve known that the clockwork Newtonian view of the physical universe turns out to be a much messier and indeterminate affair, as does the universe of the human mind.

Why, then, has so much economic theory operated with a kind of dogged Aristotelianism, insisting that the units of capitalist society, the workers, managers, investors, consumers, owners, renters, speculators, etc. behave in predictable ways? We have case after case showing that intelligence and critical reasoning often have little to do with success or failure in the market. In such cases, however, one often hears the “madness of crowds” or other clichés invoked as an explanation.

To illustrate, market reporters and business writers have seized upon the story of Isaac Newton’s spectacular rise and fall in the so-called “ South Sea Bubble ” of 1720. We find the story in Benjamin Graham’s 1949 classic The Intelligent Investor , a widely-read book that attributes the irrationality of market systems to an anthropomorphic entity named “Mr. Market.”

Back in the spring of 1720, Sir Isaac Newton owned shares in the South Sea Company, the hottest stock in England. Sensing that the market was getting out of hand, the great physicist muttered that he ‘ could calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of the people .’ Newton dumped his South Sea shares, pocketing a 100% profit totaling £7,000. But just months later, swept up in the wild enthusiasm of the market, Newton jumped back in at a much higher price — and lost £20,000 (or more than $3 million in [2002–2003’s] money. For the rest of his life, he forbade anyone to speak the words ‘South Sea’ in his presence.

The quotation in bold may or may not have been uttered by Newton, but the events Graham describes did indeed happen. As the Wall Street Journal ’s Jason Zweig relates , University of Minnesota professor Andrew Odlyzko found that “Newton had shifted from a prudent investor with his money spread across several securities to a speculator who had plunged essentially all of his capital into a single stock. The great scientist was chasing hot performance as desperately as a day trader in 1999 or many bitcoin buyers in 2017.” (Odlyzko estimates Newton’s losses at closer to $4 million.) Perhaps it was not a metaphorical “Mr. Market” who cost Newton up to 77% “on his worst purchases,” nor was it widespread “wild enthusiasm”—the mass movement of passion that Enlightenment philosophers so feared.

Perhaps it was Newton himself who, Elena Holodny writes at Business Insider , “let his emotions get the best of him, and got swayed by the irrationality of the crowd.” Maybe it’s more accurate to say Newton succumbed to greed when the bubble expanded. “Throughout history,” Barbara Kollmeyer writes at Market Watch in her interview with author Richard Dale , “people—especially those at the top rung of society—have been greedy and gullible participants in financial bubbles. And Sir Isaac Newton was only human, after all.” (How many at the top rung of society fell prey to Bernie Madoff’s schemes? And a century before the South Sea Bubble , hundreds of wealthy investors lost their shirts in the Dutch Tulip Bulb craze. )

"You may have to break your heart, but it isn’t nothing to know even one moment alive."
“You may have to break your heart, but it isn’t nothing to know even one moment alive.”

The morning after a relationship of depth and significance long bending under the weight of its own complexity had finally broken with an exhausted thud, I opened the kiln to discover a month’s worth of pottery shattered — two pieces had exploded, the shrapnel ruining the rest. All that centering, all that glazing, all the hours of pressing letterforms into the wet clay — all of it in shiny shards. And meanwhile spring was breaking outside and a little girl in bright blue rain boots was jumping in a puddle, smashing the reflections of the clouds with savage joy.
And I thought, this is all there is: breaking, breaking apart, breaking open.

It is not an easy assignment, being alive. Coming awake from the stupor of near-living that lulls us through our days, awake to the knowledge that on the other side of the neighborhood ICE trucks are handcuffing people and on the other side of the planet children are dying in gunfire, while outside the first birds of spring are singing and everywhere people are falling in love and in some faraway mountain village a shepherd is singing under a thousand stars. And somehow, somehow, all of it has to cohere into a single world in which we, in all our incohesion, must live this single life.
can be enough to make you look up
at the yellowed leaves of the apple tree, the few
that survived the rains and frost, shot
with late afternoon sun. They glow a deep
orange-gold against a blue so sheer, a single bird
would rip it like silk. You may have to break
your heart, but it isn’t nothing
to know even one moment alive. The sound
of an oar in an oarlock or a ruminant
animal tearing grass. The smell of grated ginger.
The ruby neon of the liquor store sign.
Warm socks. You remember your mother,
her precision a ceremony, as she gathered
the white cotton, slipped it over your toes,
drew up the heel, turned the cuff. A breath
can uncoil as you walk across your own muddy yard,
the big dipper pouring night down over you, and everything
you dread, all you can’t bear, dissolves
and, like a needle slipped into your vein —
that sudden rush of the world.

Complement with Henry James on how to stop waiting and start living and Hermann Hesse on how to be more alive , then revisit Ellen’s magnificent poem “How to Apologize.” And if you are looking to break your poetry open, I couldn’t recommend her Living Room Craft Talks more heartily.

The Most Powerful Attitude You Can Take Toward Your Life and the Life of the World
"This fluke, single, huge, cross-indexed, thermodynamic experiment of a story that the world has been inventing to tell itself at bedtime is still in embryo. It's not even the outline of a…

“This fluke, single, huge, cross-indexed, thermodynamic experiment of a story that the world has been inventing to tell itself at bedtime is still in embryo. It’s not even the outline of a synopsis of notes toward a rough draft yet.”

Perhaps the gravest violence we can do to ourselves is to live out our lives believing the world to be a fixity handed down to us by the authorities of history and life to be a matter of taking immutable givens. Daring to believe otherwise — to believe that even our smallest purposeful action alters the monolith of reality in some subtle, meaningful way — is an act of courage and resistance, an act of immense vulnerability to the possibility of disappointment, vulnerability the commonest cowering from which is cynicism.

James Baldwin knew this when he issued his lyrical and impassioned insistence that “nothing is fixed, forever and forever and forever, it is not fixed,” that “we made the world we’re living in and we have to make it over.”

Hannah Arendt knew this when she considered how we invent ourselves and reinvent the world , observing that “the smallest act in the most limited circumstances bears the seed of boundlessness, because one deed, and sometimes one word, suffices to change every constellation.”

Richard Powers knew this when he made his contribution to Take My Advice: Letters to the Next Generation from People Who Know a Thing or Two ( public library ) — artist and writer James L. Harmon’s wonderful 2002 anthology of wisdom from stellar minds , a decade in the constellating, envisioned as an eclectic contemporary counterpart to Rilke’s timeless Letters to a Young Poet , which had moved Harmon deeply when he first encountered it as a young man.
Two decades before Powers won the Pulitzer Prize for his sylvan symphony The Overstory , he echoes Seamus Heaney’s exhortation to always remain “true to your own secret knowledge” and writes:

Never forget what you were born knowing. That this fluke, single, huge, cross-indexed, thermodynamic experiment of a story that the world has been inventing to tell itself at bedtime is still in embryo. It’s not even the outline of a synopsis of notes toward a rough draft yet. Buy the plot some time.
We buy the plot time with the currency of our conscious choices, the grand and the mundane alike — the daily actions that make us what we are, the people who make the world what it is. Powers writes:

Take in more, consume less, recycle everything; book-keep all hidden costs; find out where you have been set down; lobby for a smaller market; get rid of your car and travel as widely as you can (yeah, walk: what the hell); try to say a little more than you mean; carry a pocket encyclopedia (ask for one without packaging) and when the entry on “Diffusion Constant” says, “for more information, see ‘Pastry War,'” see “Pastry War.”

This latter sentiment might at first appear dated in the hindsight of two decades, in the epoch of Wikipedia. But it is actually all the more insightful and urgent today, for the quiet act of resistance at its heart has grown all the harder. What I most rue about the internet is that, for all its riches of readily accessible information, it has altered the texture of human curiosity, vanquishing that wondrous encyclopedic feeling of learning about the thing you hadn’t known you didn’t know but now greatly enjoy knowing. Somewhere along the way of choices being made for us by an insular tribe of technologists, discovery was sacrificed at the altar of search as algorithms perfected the mechanics of giving us more and more of what we already knew we wanted and believed, rendering the mind itself more and more a fixity. Would you be Googling “Pastry War” now had I not made this point about a point Richard Powers made long ago on the pages of a yellowing book I pulled from my bookshelf by some incomputable human impulse this morning?
Those choices matter, Powers reminds us, even at the smallest scale. There is no fulcrum too small for the lever of change to lift from, but the lift must begin with lucidity. He writes:
The Only Three Distinctions Between People
It may be that consciousness evolved to sieve the relevant from the incomprehensible allness of all there is, to parse the world into concepts and find an organizing principle for the chaos…

It may be that consciousness evolved to sieve the relevant from the incomprehensible allness of all there is, to parse the world into concepts and find an organizing principle for the chaos of them. Our cognitive inheritance is a restless yearning to fathom how things cohere and where they belong, a yearning we have given shape to in laws and labels, weights and balances, hierarchies and categories. It has served us well, this instinct to categorize in order to contain, giving us music, the laws of planetary motion, and democracy. But it also pulsates beneath every ism we have ever invented, beneath every stereotype and every genocide, beneath every algorithm that reduces us to variables then adds them up to sell the sum of who we are, beneath all the parcels of preconception we trade daily and mistake the barter a for a genuine encounter with one another.
Two centuries ago, Nathaniel Hawthorne (July 4, 1804–May 19, 1864) offered a pithy, powerful antidote to this double-edged instinct.

In a notebook entry from the autumn of 1836, penned shortly after his moving meditation on how not to waste your life , Hawthorne proposes a revision of our standard classification system for humanity — one that would rehumanize us with the simple awareness that what binds us is infinitely stronger than what divides us or by what affiliations we divide ourselves. He writes:

A new classification of society is to be instituted. Instead of rich and poor, high and low, they are to be classed, — First, by their sorrows: for instance, whenever there are any, whether in fair mansion or hovel, who are mourning the loss of relations and friends, and who wear black, whether the cloth be coarse or superfine, they are to make one class. Secondly, all who have the same maladies, whether they lie under damask canopies or on straw pallets or in the wards of hospitals, they are to form one class. Thirdly, all who are guilty of the same sins, whether the world knows them or not; whether they languish in prison, looking forward to the gallows, or walk honored among men, they also form a class. Then proceed to generalize and classify the whole world together, as none can claim utter exemption from either sorrow, sin, or disease; and if they could, yet Death, like a great parent, comes and sweeps all through one darksome portal, — all his children.

What a magnificent way to remember that down where the spirit meets the bone , we are all facing the same struggle: to feel safe, to feel seen, to wrest some meaning and some marvel from the ephemeral bewilderment of being alive.

How to Criticize with Kindness: Philosopher Daniel Dennett on the Four Steps to Arguing Intelligently
"Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?"
“Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?”

“In disputes upon moral or scientific points,” Arthur Martine counseled in his magnificent 1866 guide to the art of conversation , “let your aim be to come at truth, not to conquer your opponent. So you never shall be at a loss in losing the argument, and gaining a new discovery.” Of course, this isn’t what happens most of the time when we argue, both online and off, but especially when we deploy the artillery of our righteousness from behind the comfortable shield of the keyboard. That form of “criticism” — which is really a menace of reacting rather than responding — is worthy of Mark Twain’s memorable remark that “the critic’s symbol should be the tumble-bug: he deposits his egg in somebody else’s dung, otherwise he could not hatch it.” But it needn’t be this way — there are ways to be critical while remaining charitable, of aiming not to “conquer” but to “come at truth,” not to be right at all costs but to understand and advance the collective understanding.

Daniel Dennett (March 28, 1942–April 19, 2024), whom artificial intelligence pioneer Marvin Minsky has called “our best current philosopher” and “the next Bertrand Russell ,” poses an apt question that probes some of the basic tendencies and dynamics of today’s everyone-is-a-critic culture: “Just how charitable are you supposed to be when criticizing the views of an opponent?”

In Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking ( public library ) — the same fantastic volume that gave us Dennett on the dignity and art-science of making mistakes — he offers what he calls “the best antidote [for the] tendency to caricature one’s opponent” : a list of rules formulated decades ago by the legendary social psychologist and game theorist Anatol Rapoport, best-known for originating the famous tit-for-tat strategy of game theory. Dennett synthesizes the steps:
How to compose a successful critical commentary:
You should attempt to re-express your target’s position so clearly, vividly, and fairly that your target says, “Thanks, I wish I’d thought of putting it that way.”
You should list any points of agreement (especially if they are not matters of general or widespread agreement).
You should mention anything you have learned from your target.
Only then are you permitted to say so much as a word of rebuttal or criticism.
If only the same code of conduct could be applied to critical commentary online, particularly to the indelible inferno of comments.

But rather than a naively utopian, Pollyannaish approach to debate, Dennett points out this is actually a sound psychological strategy that accomplishes one key thing: It transforms your opponent into a more receptive audience for your criticism or dissent, which in turn helps advance the discussion.
Compare and contrast with Susan Sontag’s three steps to refuting any argument , and treat yourself to Dennett’s wholly excellent Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking .

The Relief of Rock Bottom: George Orwell and the Secret Springboard of Success
It happens to everyone — to kings and paupers, to astronauts and poets. Nothing will protect you from it — not money, not love, not perfect health — for it spares no life that is fully…

It happens to everyone — to kings and paupers, to astronauts and poets. Nothing will protect you from it — not money, not love, not perfect health — for it spares no life that is fully lived, not the sunniest or the most privileged or the best planned.

It begins with the wall — the one you hit over and over and over, not breaking through. And then, after the exhausted collapse, the bottom. The floorboards of despair, cold as granite, absolute as gravity.

But then something extraordinary happens — something George Orwell (June 25, 1903–January 21, 1950) captures perfectly in a passage from Down and out in Paris and London ( public library ), recounting his experience of abject poverty while trying to become a writer, working in restaurant kitchens in Paris and wandering London as a tramp.
What Orwell observes of material poverty applies equally to the spiritual poverty of hope and meaning we call despair:

When you are approaching poverty, you make one discovery which outweighs some of the others. You discover boredom and mean complications and the beginnings of hunger, but you also discover the great redeeming feature of poverty: the fact that it annihilates the future.

It annihilates, he means, anxiety about the future, for when you have nothing left to lose, there is nothing to worry about losing. That is the relief of rock bottom — a feeling that is “a great consolation” when you are at your lowest, and one that “everyone who has been hard up has experienced”:

It is a feeling of relief, almost of pleasure, at knowing yourself at last genuinely down and out. You have talked so often of going to the dogs — and well, here are the dogs, and you have reached them, and you can stand it. It takes off a lot of anxiety.
Two millennia before him, Marcus Aurelius had anchored his meditation on turning suffering into strength in the same premise:

Be like a headland: the waves beat against it continuously, but it stands fast and around it the boiling water dies down. “It’s my rotten luck that this has happened to me.” On the contrary, “It’s my good luck that, although this has happened to me, I still feel no distress, since I’m unbruised by the present and unconcerned about the future.” What happened could have happened to anyone, but not everyone could have carried on without letting it distress him.
Here, the Stoic perspective converges with the Buddhist, best articulated by Pema Chödrön in her timeless field guide to transformation through trying times :
Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over to annihilation can that which is indestructible be found in us.

And that is the thing about rock bottom: Not only does it hold, but it is there you discover the part of you that also holds — the bedrock of your being unassailable by all the loss, all the failure, all the frivolities of chance. Orwell, being neither a Stoic nor a Buddhist, understood the universality of his experience. “It is a fairly trivial story,” he writes at the end of his memoir — trivial because its essence is so common, no matter the guise; trivial because it touches an elemental truth: The relief of rock bottom is not that you have sunk to it but that, having survived it, you can only rise.

The manuscript of Orwell’s memoir was twice rejected, including by T.S. Eliot at Faber & Faber. In a fit of despair, Orwell tossed it into his friend Mabel’s garbage bin. She fished it out and, without his knowledge, took it to a literary agent she knew. We could say that the rest is history, but the selective collective memory we call history is an erasure machine for the myriad failures behind every success, for the rock bottom that is so often — so much oftener than our culture likes to admit — the springboard for the redemption of our suffering.

How Magic Lantern Ghosts Helped Measure the Stars
A nineteenth-century invention brought theatrical illusions into the observatory, changing how astronomers studied starlight.

In the nineteenth century, entertainers began dazzling audiences with the “magic lantern.” Operators used these projection systems to bring marvelous images to large crowds. They even performed tricks on the eye, conjuring “ghosts” onto the stage using reflections or transparent screens. But some at the time saw scientific possibilities in those ghostly images.

The rise of projection culture coincided with an increasing effort to mechanize astronomy . Astronomers had been precisely charting the positions of stars and other objects, and the next step was to study their color and brightness. German projectionist Karl Friedrich Zöllner realized that magic lanterns might help astronomers in this effort, explains historian Klaus Staubermann . He argues that Zöllner’s new scientific instrument, an astro-photometer, harnessed the subjective perception created by the magic lantern for scientific purposes.

The principles behind the “magic lantern” have a deep history, but improvements by Christiaan Huygens and others in the seventeenth century led to more widespread use. Staubermann describes how magic lanterns became popular lecture aids by the eighteenth century, as improvements to lighting and mirrors made them suitable for larger theaters. Projectionists learned new ways to control brightness and create visual effects using a variety of filters and lenses. Meanwhile, scientists were experimenting with optics, prisms, and mineralogy.

It was in this milieu that Zöllner became a projectionist and a student of photometry. He began studying illusions, trying to understand how we distinguish them from reality. He thought of the retina itself as a projection screen, Staubermann explains. To Zöllner, “The mind was the spectator,” he writes, “looking at the image and deciding what of that which was seen was illusory and what was real.”
The Hidden Aesthetics of Early Astrophotography
Behind the transformative star photographs of the 1880s lay a complex collaboration between astronomers and engravers.

It was the interplay between reality and illusion that enabled Zöllner’s photometer. The instrument employed techniques similar to those used to conjure ghosts on the stage to create artificial stars. A gas burner provided intense and steady light, which was projected as a point of light on a semi-transparent glass screen using lenses and prisms.

“For the observer with a Zöllner photometer,” Staubermann writes, “it appeared as if both stars were actually in the sky, having the same background.” The operator could control the brightness of the “ghost” star and compare it with a real one. Previously, astronomers’ perceptions of star brightness and color varied, sometimes significantly. But as they began experimenting with Zöllner’s photometer, they obtained results that agreed with each other.

The instrument became a best seller in Europe and the United States. Astronomers added it to telescopes like the one at Leipzig Observatory. By the 1870s, Staubermann explains, “of the observatories participating in international observing programmes almost half of them had ordered a Zöllner photometer.” Papers on astro-photometry proliferated, and Zöllner himself became the first German professor of astrophysics.

Staubermann argues that the photometer didn’t quite make astro-photometry a “mechanically objective” science, however. Using it meant refining observation skills rather than eliminating the need for them. “Through the use of Zöllner’s photometer,” he writes, “observers learned how to both control and improve their visual judgement.”
